Borrowed from Latin acrōtērium, from Ancient Greek ἀκρωτήριον (akrōtḗrion).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin addictus and adapted to native detto.

parole.significato: to suit, to be becoming, to be suitable
parole.testo: Possibly from Latin ad- + decere (“to be suitable”), subsequently remodelled after Italian dire (“to say”) and given the impersonal ending -si. Compare disdire (“to not suit”).

parole.significato: to carry out, to accomplish, to implement, to perform
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin adimpleō from ad- + impleō (“fill up; satisfy”).
From Latin adhaerēre (“to cleave, stick to”).

Borrowed from Latin adhaesum, supine of adhaereō (“to cleave or stick to”).

parole.significato: masterless, ownerless (lacking a master or owner)

parole.significato: to love with one's entire heart and soul; regard with deep respect and affection
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adōrāre. Cf. the older aorare.

parole.significato: to adsorb (to accumulate on a surface, by adsorption)
parole.testo: Alternative form of assorbire, from Latin adsorbēre.

parole.significato: to flatter, to adulate, to soft-soap
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adūlārī. Compare Spanish and Portuguese adular.

parole.significato: to assemble or gather (people); to muster; to round up

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āerem (“air”). Compare Sicilian aira. See also aria.
From Latin aphaca, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: to declare, to affirm, to state, to claim, to assert

parole.testo: From Latin affirmātīvus. By surface analysis, affermare + -ivo.

Borrowed from Latin afflīgere. Compare French affliger, Spanish afligir and English afflict, which were also all borrowed.
Borrowed from Latin affluere with change of conjugation.

parole.significato: to pant, to gasp, to wheeze

parole.significato: to attack, to assault, to assail, to mug

parole.significato: The plot-relevant reveal of a character's previously unknown identity.

parole.significato: bubo that occurs especially in the groin
parole.testo: From Latin inguen (“groin”) possibly crossed phonetically with anguis (“snake”), possibly through a Medieval Latin anguen.

parole.significato: agon (all senses); contest, competition, litigation; battlefield
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agōn, from Ancient Greek ἀγών (agṓn).
From Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “gathering of people or place of gathering”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: a grape variety that does not reach maturation

parole.testo: From earlier *acrifoglio, from Latin acrifolium, from acer (“bitter, sharp”) + folium (“leaf”). Compare Catalan grèvol, Occitan grefuèlh, agrèvol, Franco-Provençal agriblon. Cf. also aquifolium, whence Spanish acebo, Portuguese azevinho.

parole.significato: Agrigentine (of, from or relating to the city of Agrigento, Sicily, Italy)
parole.testo: From Latin agrigentīnus, from Agrigentum (“Agrigento”) + -īnus. By surface analysis, Agrigento + -ino (relation suffix).
Borrowed from Latin agrum, from Proto-Italic *agros, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros.

parole.significato: barnyard, farmyard, threshing floor; paved area (typical of case coloniche) used to thresh wheat, shell legumes and dry…

From Aiace (“Ajax”, the Greek mythological hero said to have been turned into a hyacinth after taking his own life), from Latin Aiācem, from Ancient Greek Αἴας (Aías).
Inherited from Latin āreola, diminutive of ārea (“open space”). By surface analysis, aia (“threshing floor”) + -ola (diminutive suffix). Compare borrowed doublet areola. Compare Sicilian ariu.

From Latin alabastrum, or borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros), from earlier ἀλάβαστος (alábastos, “vase made of alabaster”).
Ultimately from Latin allēc (“fish sauce”). (Compare Catalan alatxa.) Doublet of alice.
Borrowed from Latin alacrem (“lively, brisk; happy”). Doublet of allegro.
Learned borrowing from Latin alauda, borrowed from Gaulish *alauda (“skylark”, literally “tuft”). Synonym and doublet of allodola.
From Latin arborētum (keeping pace with the changes undergone by albero < arborem). By surface analysis, albero (“tree”) + -eta.

Borrowed from Latin albicāre, derived from albus (“white”).

From Latin albus (“white”), possibly taken as a learned term (first attested 14th century), from Proto-Italic *alβos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elbʰós.

From Latin alcyōn, from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn, “kingfisher”).

From Latin algōrem (“cold”), from the verb algeō (“to be, feel cold”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *h₂elgʰ- (“frost, cold”).

parole.significato: any bird of the genus Haliaeetus

parole.significato: allocution, speech, tirade, sermon, diatribe, harangue

From Latin antarcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós, “opposite the arctic”).

From Latin antrum (“cave”). Compare French antre, Portuguese and Spanish antro.

Calque of Latin cāsus rēctus, in turn a calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθή πτῶσις (orthḗ ptôsis). Literally, “straight/direct case”.
From Latin casula, a diminutive of casa.
Borrowed from Latin Caspius, from Ancient Greek Κάσπιος (Káspios).
Inherited from Latin capsa. Doublet of capsa.

From Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia).
Inherited from Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum.

parole.significato: to punish, to castigate (in order to correct)

parole.testo: From Latin castīgātōrem. By surface analysis, castigare + -tore.

parole.significato: chaste (abstaining from immoral or unlawful sexual intercourse)
parole.testo: Uncertain if inherited or borrowed from Latin castus.
From an older castore, from Latin castōrem, from Ancient Greek Κάστωρ (Kástōr).
From Latin cata-, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “under”).
From Latin cataphracta, from Ancient Greek κατάφρακτης (katáphraktēs).

From Latin catasta, from Ancient Greek κατάστασις (katástasis, “establishment, institution, method, condition”).

Latin catēchīzāre (“to instruct in religion; to catechize”), from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to instruct orally”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to resound, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).
Borrowed from Latin catēnāre (“to chain together”), derived from catēna (“chain”).
Borrowed from Latin catēnātus, perfect participle of catēnō (“to chain together”), derived from catēna (“chain”).
From Latin cathetus, from Ancient Greek κάθετος (káthetos). The forwarding of the accent may be explained as a false analogy with the suffix -eto from Latin -ētum (“a grove of ...”).
From Latin catilīnārius (“pertaining to Catiline”). By surface analysis, Catilina + -ario (“-ary”).

parole.significato: one who is austere and of strict conduct; martinet
parole.testo: From Catone, from Latin Catōnem, name of Cato the Elder (234 ca. BCE–149 BCE), known for his proverbial strictness, and Cato the Younger (95 BCE–46 BCE), known as a fierce defender of the freedom of the Republic.
From Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “above”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “chair”).
Inherited from Latin captīvus (“captive” → “caught by the devil” → “bad”). Compare the semantic development of French chétif (“puny, scrawny”) and Galician cativo.
Borrowed from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós).
Borrowed from Latin caudālis, from cauda. See also coda.
Borrowed from Latin caulis. See also cavolo.
Borrowed from Latin causa. Doublet of the inherited cosa. Cognates include English and French cause, Portuguese and Spanish causa.
From Latin causātiōnem. By surface analysis, causa(re) (“to cause”) + -zione (“-tion”).
From Latin cautus, derived from caveō (“to beware, avoid”).
Borrowed from Latin cautiōnem (“precaution, caution”), derived from caveō (“to beware, avoid”).

parole.significato: to take out, pull out, or extract forcefully

parole.testo: From Latin cavātiō, from cavō (“I hollow out”).

parole.significato: the seats in ancient theatres and amphitheatres
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cavea. Doublet of gaggia and gabbia.

From Latin clavicula via early syncope of unstressed intertonic /ŭ/ and then loss of the first /l/ via dissimilation from the second. Doublet of caviglia, borrowed from Occitan, and clavicola, borrowed from Latin.
From Latin cavum, cavus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”).

parole.significato: to withdraw, to surrender, to give up

Borrowed from Latin cēphus, from Ancient Greek κῆπος (kêpos), alternative form of κῆβος (kêbos, “long-tailed monkey”).

Learned borrowing from Latin celer, celerem.

From Latin Celticus, from Ancient Greek Κελτῐκός (Keltĭkós). By surface analysis, celta + -ico.

From Latin cinerem, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”).
Inherited from Latin cinericius. By surface analysis, cenere + -iccio.
From Latin cingulum. Compare the doublets cingolo and cinghia.
From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

parole.testo: From cento + pelle. Or linked Latin centipelliō, centipellium, from centum + pellis; cf. Romanian cimpoi (“bagpipe”).
Borrowed from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”). The nonstandard pronunciation with -é- might be due to influence of entrare.

parole.significato: a member of the centumviri in ancient Rome

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cippus. Doublet of cippo, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin cērāre (“to smear or coat with wax”), from cēra (“wax”).
From Latin cerasus, from Ancient Greek κερασός (kerasós).
Learned borrowing from Latin cerastēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κεράστης (kerástēs).
From Latin circulus, which is derived from circus. Cognate to the borrowed doublet circolo.

parole.significato: tightly-coiled cloth pad placed on the head to support loads
parole.testo: From the older cercino, from Latin circinus.
From Latin Cereālis (“relating to Ceres”), from Cerēs (“goddess of agriculture”).

Inherited from Latin cēreus. Doublet of cereo.

From Latin cervus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂wós, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“horn”).

parole.significato: a fermented beverage similar to beer
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cervēs(i)a. First attested as cervese in 1252/8; cervogia is documented from 1348 onwards. The forms with /ˈi/ may come directly from Latin; those with /ˈe/ or /ˈo/ seem to reflect the Old French cerveise~cervoise.

parole.significato: of Julius Caesar or the gens Julia; Caesarean
parole.testo: From Latin Caesareus (“pertaining to Caesar”). By surface analysis, Cesare (“Caesar”) + -eo (“-ean”).

parole.significato: a temple dedicated to Caesar Augustus or another emperor
parole.testo: From Latin caesareum, substantivized neuter form of caesareus (“pertaining to Caesar”). By surface analysis, Cesare (“Caesar”) + -eo (“-ean”).

parole.significato: Caesarean (of or relating to Julius Caesar)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Caesariānus. By surface analysis, Cesare + -iano.

parole.significato: a source of income or earnings: an asset

parole.significato: to hush, to silence, to quiet

parole.significato: he/she/they who, those who, the ones who; (archaic) whom

parole.significato: edible seed, bean, grain, etc. from a plant

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of Chieti, Abruzzo, Italy

From Latin clīnāre (“to slope or incline; to bend; to sink”), from Proto-Italic *kl(e)inō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.

Learned borrowing from Latin cicatrīcem, cicatricem.

parole.testo: From Latin Cicerōnem, agnomen of Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator, from cicer (“chickpea”), a reference to his warts, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱiker- (“pea”). By surface analysis, Latin Cicero + -one (agentive suffix).

Borrowed from Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós), derived from κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).

From Latin cicōnia, derived from Proto-Indo-European *kekoh₂n-, from the root *keh₂n- (“to sing”).

parole.significato: Cydonian (of, from or relating to Cydonia (ancient city-state in Crete))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cydōnius, from Ancient Greek Κυδώνιος (Kudṓnios), derived from Κυδωνίᾱ (Kudōníā).
From Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”).
From Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.
From Latin cilium, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel-yo-m, which is derived from *ḱel- (“to cover”).

parole.testo: Derived from Latin cygnus, derived from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).

From Latin cȳmatium, from Ancient Greek κυμάτιον (kumátion, “small wave”).

parole.significato: mixture or concoction used by goldsmiths to purify or assay precious metals

From Latin cypērus, from Ancient Greek κύπειρος (kúpeiros).
Perhaps from vulgar forms like *sorcipiglio, *sorpiciglio, from Latin supercilium (“frown”). Compare sopracciglio (“eyebrow”).

parole.significato: an engraved stone serving as a memorial or marking a boundary, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cippus. Doublet of ceppo, which was inherited.

parole.significato: Cyprian, Cypriot (chiefly in reference to Greek mythology)
parole.testo: From Latin Cyprius, from Ancient Greek Κύπριος (Kúprios).

Borrowed from Latin circulus. Cognate to the inherited doublet cerchio.

Borrowed from Latin circumfulgēre, with change of conjugation.

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin circumvolvere (“to cause to roll around”). Adapted to volgere.
From Latin circumscrībere, from circum (“around”) + scrībō (“to write”) (compare scrivere).
Borrowed from Latin circumscrīptiōnem (“outline”). Compare French circonscription (“electoral district”).
From circum- + navigare or borrowed from Latin circumnāvigāre (“to circumnavigate”), from circum (“around, about”) + nāvigō (“sail, navigate”).

Borrowed from Latin cīvem, from Proto-Italic *keiwis (“society”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱéy-wo-s (“intimate, friendly”), derived from the root *ḱey- (“to settle”).

Borrowed from Latin claudicantem, present active participle of claudicō (“to limp”).

From Latin clērus, from Ancient Greek κλῆρος (klêros).

Borrowed from Latin clūnem (“buttock”), from Proto-Italic *klounis, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlównis (“buttocks, hip”).

parole.significato: to cohabit, to cohabitate (to share a dwelling)

parole.significato: collection (gathering of money for charitable or other purposes)

From Latin liquiritia, from Ancient Greek γλῠκύρριζα (glŭkúrrhiza), from γλῠκύς (glŭkús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”). Compare Sicilian rigulizzia.
From Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρᾱ (lúrā).
Borrowed from Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós).
From Latin lyristēs, from Ancient Greek λυριστής (luristḗs). By surface analysis, lira + -ista.

From Latin lixīvia, variant of lixīva, noun use of the adjective lixīvus (“made into lye”), from the use aqua lixīva. Compare Portuguese lixívia, French lessive, Friulian lissie, Sardinian lissía and liscìa, Sicilian lissìa and liscìa, Spanish lejía, Romanian leșie.
Possibly from Latin ēlīsus, past participle of ēlīdere.

parole.significato: to quarrel, to fight, to argue [with con ‘with someone’]
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lītigāre. Compare Spanish lidiar and Portuguese lidar.

parole.significato: quarrel, row, altercation, tiff, squabble, toil, strife

parole.testo: From Latin lītus, lītoris + -āneus (compare Portuguese litorâneo).
From Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía).

parole.significato: level (tool for finding whether a surface is level)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin lībella (“small balance”), from lībra (“balance”). First attested before 1504.
Inherited from Latin lĭbellus (literally “little book”), then "written act, document".
Borrowed from Latin līvidus, an adjective derived from the verb līveō (“to be blueish or livid”).

parole.significato: a military leader of an armed band
parole.testo: From Latin lochāgus, from Ancient Greek λοχᾱγός (lokhāgós), derived from λόχος (lókhos, “a file in the phalanx”).
Diminutive of Latin locanda, from locandus (“which is to be placed”). Compare locanda (“inn”).

parole.significato: to rent, to let, to hire

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin illōc but influenced in its form by Etymology 1.

parole.significato: lochus (a military unit headed by a lochagus)
parole.testo: From Latin lochus, from Ancient Greek λόχος (lókhos).
Internationalism. Ultimately an unadapted borrowing from Latin locus (“place, spot”). Doublet of luogo.
Borrowed from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin. Doublet of the inherited aragosta.
From Latin laudāre, whence also Italian laudare (a borrowed doublet).
From lodare + -tore, or from Latin laudātōrem.
From Latin laudem, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lēwt-, *lēwdʰ- (“song, sound”), from *lēw- (“to sound, resound, sing out”).
Inherited from Latin laudābilis. By surface analysis, lodare + -evole. Compare borrowed doublet laudabile.
Inherited from Latin lolium. Compare Portuguese joio, Spanish joyo and Catalan jull.

parole.significato: logomachy (dispute over the meaning of a word)
parole.testo: From the Latin logomachia, from the Ancient Greek λογομαχία (logomakhía).
From Latin logicus. Doublet of logico.
From earlier *lop'la, contraction of *lopola, *loppola, diminutive of loppa (“rind, bark, peel”), ultimately from Latin loba.

From Latin lumbus, possibly through Osco-Umbrian (as the expected Latin form would be *lundus), from Proto-Italic *lonðwos, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰwos, from the root *lendʰ- (“to enter, penetrate, expand”). Cognate with Old English lynd (“fat, grease”), Old English lendenu (“loins”). More at

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of London, capital of England and the United Kingdom
parole.testo: From Latin Londīnēnsis, from Londīnium (“London”) + -ēnsis (“ese”). Compare Italian Londra, -ese. Cognate to Spanish londinense.
Borrowed from Latin longitūdinem (“length, longitude”), from longus (“long”).
Uncertain; often suggested to be from derived from Latin lūridus (“sallow, pale”), via Late Latin lurdus, making it a doublet of lurido.
Inherited from Latin illōrum, genitive plural of ille, illud (“that”).
Inherited from Latin luscus. Cognate in particular with French louche, with whom it shares the semantic shift to describe a shady individual.
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).
Inherited from Latin lutum, derived from luō (“to wash, cleanse”). Doublet of luto.
From lottare + -tore, or from Latin luctātōrem.
Borrowed from Latin lōtiōnem, from lavō.
From Latin lūbricus, possibly a borrowing.

parole.significato: light (visible electromagnetic wave; electrical device providing light)
parole.testo: From Latin lūcem (“light”), from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“bright; white”). Doublet of the borrowed lux.
Inherited from Latin lūcēre, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“to shine”).
From Latin lacertula, diminutive of lacerta (“lizard”). Doublet of alligatore. Compare Galician, Spanish, and Portuguese lagarto (“lizard”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lūciferum, from lūx (“light”) + -fer (“bearing, bringing”), a calque on Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros). Doublet of Lucifero.

From Latin lūcus (“grove sacred to a deity”), from Old Latin loucos, from Proto-Indo-European *lowkós (“open space, clearing”), derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include English lea (“meadow”), Hindi लोक (lok, “public” ← “world”), Lithuanian laũkas (“field”).
From Latin lūculentus, derived from lūx (“light”).
From Latin Luculliānus, named for Lucullus, a Roman general known for the lavish feasts that he gave; see also English Lucullan.
Borrowed from Latin lucumōnem, form of lucumō, from Etruscan 𐌋𐌀𐌖𐌊𐌖𐌌 (laukum).
A Dantean Latinism borrowed from Latin lūdere (“to play”), of disputed origin.
From Latin lūgubris (“mournful; gloomy”), possibly a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin lūmen. In the sense of "lumen" it is a modern neologism. Doublet of lumen, a borrowing.
Inherited from Latin lūmināre (“to illuminate, brighten”).

parole.significato: lighting effects (art and practice of, on stage and in film/TV)

parole.testo: From Luna, from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).

parole.significato: lunar (of or pertaining to the moon)

parole.testo: From Latin lūnātus (“curved; crescent- or half-moon-shaped”).
From Latin Lūnae dīēs, variant of dīēs Lūnae (“day of the Moon”).
From Latin longus (“long, extended”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).
From earlier luoco < loco, from Latin locus.
Borrowed from Latin lupīnus. By surface analysis, lupo + -ino.
Borrowed from Latin lupus. Doublet of lovo and the inherited lupo.
Borrowed from Latin lupus in fabula.
Borrowed from Latin lūridus (“pale yellow, wan, sallow; ghastly”). Compare the inherited doublet lordo (“dirty”).
Derived from Latin luscus (“one-eyed, half blind”)
From Latin lūxāre (“to put out of joint, dislocate”) (possibly a semi-learned borrowing), cognate with Ancient Greek λοξός (loxós, “slanting”).

parole.significato: to be luxuriant, to flourish (of plants)
parole.testo: Calque of Latin lūxuriāre, from lussuria + -eggiare.
Borrowed from Latin lustrāre (“to purify; to examine”).
Borrowed from Latin lutum, derived from luō (“to wash, cleanse”). Compare the inherited doublet loto.
From Latin lūctus. Compare Spanish and Portuguese luto.
From Latin illāc. Compare Spanish allá, Portuguese lá, French là, Sicilian ḍḍà. The original geminated -ll-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.
From Latin illic. Compare Spanish allí, Portuguese ali. The original geminated -ll-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.
Borrowed from Latin machina (“engine, device, mill”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Compare the inherited doublet macina (“grindstone”).

parole.significato: to plot, to contrive, to machinate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin māchinārī (“scheme, plot”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Morphological doublet of macinare, an inherited form.
From macchia + -oso, or from Latin maculōsus.
Inherited from Latin macellārius. By surface analysis, macello + aio. Compare Romanian măcelar.
From Latin macellum, related to Ancient Greek μάκελλον (mákellon), μάκελλος (mákellos).
Inherited from Latin machina (“device, mill”). Doublet of macchina (“machine, car”), which was borrowed.
Ultimately from Latin māchina (“device”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Cf. Late Latin māchinula (“little device”).
Learned borrowing from Latin macrum (“lean, skinny”). Doublet of magro.
Borrowed from Latin macula, whence also the inherited doublet macchia.
Borrowed from Latin madidus, derived from madeō (“to be wet or moist”).

parole.significato: honorific title used to address women
moisture that covers the body prior to sweating
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin madōrem, derived from madeō (“to be wet or moist”).
From the older form matre, from Latin mātrem, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Latin magistrum. Doublet of mastro.

parole.significato: May (fifth month of the Gregorian calendar)

parole.testo: From Latin maior, maius, comparative of magnus (“big”, “great”).

parole.significato: to increase, to raise (prices, wages, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin maiōrāre (“to augment”), derived from maior (“greater”).
From Latin maiōrem /majjoːrɛ̃/, accusative case of maior, from Proto-Italic *magjōs, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂yós, from *méǵh₂s (“big”, “great”).
From Latin magicus, from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós).
Borrowed from Latin magma, from Ancient Greek μάγμα (mágma).
Borrowed from Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”).

parole.significato: magnetic (in both the scientific and figurative senses)
parole.testo: From Latin magnēticus, from Ancient Greek Μαγνητικός (Magnētikós), from Μάγνης (Mágnēs).
Borrowed from Latin magnificāre (“praise, glorify, extol”).

Unadapted borrowing from Latin magnificat, 3ʳᵈ-person present active indicative of magnificō (“to praise, glorify”). The familiar sense comes from a jocular influence from magnare, variant of mangiare (“to eat”).
Borrowed from Latin magnitūdinem. Doublet of magnitudo.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin magnitūdinem. Doublet of magnitudine.
Uncertain if inherited or semi-borrowed from Latin magnus, from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, derived from *méǵh₂s (“big; great”).
From Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos).
From Latin maiālis, from the goddess Maia.
From Latin malacia, from Ancient Greek μαλακία (malakía, “softness, sickness”).

parole.significato: bad faith, or an intent to deceive
parole.testo: From Latin mala fides; cognate with Piedmontese malafaj, malafé.

parole.significato: malanders, a scurfy eruption in the bend of the knee of the foreleg of a horse
parole.testo: From Latin malandria (“blisters or pustules on the neck, especially in horses”). Compare, for more, malanno and malestro.
From Latin malefacere. Compare French malfaire.
Past participle of malfare, corresponding to male + fatto, or from Latin malefactus.
Inherited from Latin male grātus (“ungrateful”). By surface analysis, mal(e) + grado. Cognate with Catalan malgrat and French malgré. Compare di buongrado and the borrowing grato.
From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).
Borrowed from Latin malitiōsus. By surface analysis, malizia (“malice”) + -oso.
From Latin manum (“hand”) + levāre (“raise”). Compare manlevare.
From Latin mālobathrum, from Ancient Greek μᾱλάβαθρον (mālábathron).

parole.significato: mortar (mixture of lime or cement, sand, and water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin maltha, from Ancient Greek μάλθα (máltha).
From Latin malva, of Semitic origin.
Inherited from Latin mancus, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂n-ko- (“maimed in the hand”), from *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én- (“hand”).
From Latin mandra (“column of cattle”), from Ancient Greek μάνδρα (mándra, “cattle enclosure”).
Inherited from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of mangiare, manicare, and manucare.
From Latin mamphur (“a kind of tool”).
Inherited from Latin manganum, itself from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon).
From Latin manes (“spirits of the dead”).
Borrowed from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).

parole.significato: a waxen votive image, usually hung from altars
parole.testo: From Latin imāginem. Doublet of immagine and imago.
Inherited from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manucare, and mangiare.

parole.significato: to express, to reveal (an idea, opinion, doubt, intention, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin manifēstāre (“to exhibit, make public”), derived from manifēstus (“apparent, palpable”).

parole.significato: handful (especially a small group of soldiers)

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin manus (whence also English manual, etc.), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry).
From Latin manū scrīptus, manū scrīptum (literally “written by hand”). Cognate with Piedmontese manoscrit.
Inherited from Latin manuālis. Doublet of manuale, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin mānsiōnem. Doublet of magione.
From Latin mantēllum (“covering, cloak”), diminutive of mantum, probably from Gaulish. Compare French manteau.

parole.significato: bellows - of a furnace or an organ
mantissa (part of a logarithm after the decimal point)
to crumple or rumple with the hands, to handle carelessly, to manhandle
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Latin manū trūsāre (literally “to thrust with the hand”).
Borrowed from Latin manuālem. Doublet of manovale.
Inherited from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manicare, and mangiare.
From Latin mappa, of possibly Semitic origin.
From amarasca, from amaro (“bitter”), from Latin amārus (“bitter”).
From marasca (“morello cherry”) + -ino (“diminutive suffix”), from amarasca, from amaro (“bitter”), from Latin amārus.
Derived ultimately from Latin marcēre (“rot”). Perhaps directly a deverbal of Italian marcire.
Inherited from Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.
From earlier margarita, from Latin margarīta, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs), from a loanword of Eastern origin.

parole.significato: margin, border, edge, brink, bank, brow

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin marīnus. By surface analysis, mare + -ino.

parole.significato: to cause (usually a woman) to get married, to give a husband to (someone), to marry (someone) (with a man)
name of several species of insects in the Dermestes taxonomic genus, especially the larder beetle (Dermestes lardarius)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin vermiculus, diminutive of vermis (“worm”). Considering its highly unusual development, perhaps borrowed via a regional language of Italy.
From Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros).
From Latin marum, from Ancient Greek μᾶρον (mâron).
From Latin marsūpium (“pouch”), from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion), diminutive of μάρσιππος (mársippos, “pouch”), perhaps of Oriental origin.
From Latin Martis dīēs, variant of dīēs Martis (“day of Mars”).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to the god Mars
parole.testo: From Latin Mārtius, derived from Mārs.
Borrowed from Latin masculus. Doublet of maschio.
From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
From Latin masticāre, borrowed from Ancient Greek μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to grind the teeth”).
From Latin mastiche, from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē), from μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to chew”). Compare masticare.
Older form of maestro, from Latin magistrum.

parole.significato: a sheepskin or goatskin jacket, particularly one worn by Sardinian shepherds
parole.testo: From Latin mastrūca, of Nuragic origin. Cognate with Sardinian mastruca, mastrucca.
From Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa). Cognate to French matasse, Portuguese madeixa, Spanish madeja, Romanian mătase.
From Latin māter, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
Latinization of older matera, from Latin māteria.
From Latin māternus. Doublet of Maderno (“a village in Lombardy”).
Borrowed from Latin mātrimus, derived from māter (“mother”).
From Latin mātrōna (“matron”), from māter (“mother; matron”).
From Latin mātrōnālis. By surface analysis, matrona + -ale.
Inherited from Latin mactāre. Possibly a cognate to Spanish matar.
Inherited from Latin mātūrus, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”).
Either from Latin mateola or formed as a diminutive of mazza.
Borrowed from Latin meāre (“to go along”).
From Latin moechus, from Ancient Greek μοιχός (moikhós).
From Latin Caius Maecenas, name of a well-known Roman knight (69 - 8 BC), advisor to Augustus and influential protector of writers and artists.
Inherited from Latin mēcum (probably through Old Italian conmeco), from Latin cum mēcum.
From Latin mēcōnium (“opium; excrement of a newborn child”), from Ancient Greek μηκώνιον (mēkṓnion, “poppy-juice, opium”), from μήκων (mḗkōn, “poppy”).
From Latin mēta (“boundary limit”), from Proto-Italic *mētā, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”). Doublet of meta.
Borrowed from Latin mediānus, whence also mezzano (an inherited doublet).

parole.significato: common servant employed on general duties, drudge, menial worker

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mediātōrem. Doublet of mezzadro.
Inherited from Latin medicus. Compare Neapolitan miedeco.
Borrowed from Latin medius, whence also Italian mezzo (an inherited doublet).
From Latin mēdismus, from Ancient Greek μηδισμός (mēdismós).
Borrowed from Latin meditor (“to meditate, to reflect on”), frequentative of medeor (“to cure, to heal”), influenced by Ancient Greek μελετάω (meletáō, “to cure, to reflect on, to meditate”).
From Latin meditātiōne(m), case form of meditātiō (“thinking, contemplation”). By surface analysis, medita(re) (“to meditate”) + -zione (“-ation”).
Borrowed from Latin Mēdus, from Ancient Greek Μῆδος (Mêdos), from an Iranian language.
From Latin melius. Cognate with Sicilian megghiu.
Inherited from Late Latin mēla, from mēlum, from Latin mālum, likely from Doric Greek μᾶλον (mâlon, “apple”); compare Attic μῆλον (mêlon).
From Latin māla cotōnea, from the plural of mālum cotōneum (“quince tree”), from Ancient Greek μηλοκυδώνιον (mēlokudṓnion).
From Latin armeniaca (“apricot tree”), derived from Armenia.
Borrowed from Latin melos, from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos).

parole.significato: member (one who belongs to a group; an element of a set)
parole.testo: From Latin membrum (“member; limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *memso-, *mems-ro (“flesh”).

parole.significato: memory, recall (the ability of the brain to record information)
a kind of drift net for catching sardines
parole.testo: Uncertain. Maybe from Latin maena (“small sea fish”).
From Latin mināre, collateral form of minārī.
Borrowed from Latin mendācem (“mendacious, lying, false”).

parole.significato: menologium, a monthly record, particularly in certain Christian contexts

parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Latin mēnsa (“table”), although some sources disagree.
From Latin mentha, from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).

parole.significato: a healthy body is a healthy mind
parole.testo: Calque of Latin mens sana in corpore sano. Compare French un esprit sain dans un corps sain.
From Latin mente captus (“insane”, “mad”, literally “seized by the mind”).
From Latin mentum, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to project”).

parole.significato: wonder, astonishment, amazement, surprise; feeling of wonder
to trade, to deal, to haggle
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mercārī (“to trade, deal”).
Borrowed from Latin mercēnārius or a latinization of older (and possibly inherited) mercenaio.
From Latin amāracus, amāracum (“marjoram”), from Ancient Greek ἀμᾱ́ρακος (amā́rakos), ἀμᾱ́ρακον (amā́rakon).
From Latin Mercuriī diēs, variant of diēs Mercuriī (“day of Mercury”).
Inherited from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).
From Latin merenda (“light evening meal”). Compare Galician and Portuguese merenda, Spanish merienda.
Related to standard Italian meriggiare, meriggio (“midday”). From Latin merīdiāre.
Borrowed from Latin merīdiōnālis. Cf. also the older Italian meriggionale.

parole.significato: to rest in the shade (in the afternoon)

parole.testo: From Latin meritus, perfect passive participle of mereō (“to earn, deserve”).
From Latin meritum (“merit”, “deserts”), from a noun use of the neuter form of meritus.
From Latin miscēre (“to mix”). Compare Portuguese mexer (“to move; fiddle with”), Spanish mecer (“to rock, cradle”), obsolete Romanian mește (“to pour out a drink; offer”).
From Latin mēnsem (“month”). Compare Catalan mes, French mois, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.
Borrowed from Latin mesolabium, from Ancient Greek μεσόλαβος (mesólabos).
Learned borrowing from Latin messōrem (“reaper”), derived from messus, perfect passive participle of metō (“to reap, harvest”).

parole.significato: trade, craft, job, occupation, profession, work
parole.testo: From an older *mistiere, *ministerie, from Latin ministerium (“service”), from minister (“servant”), whence also ministro. Compare French métier.
Either borrowed from Latin menstruus (“monthly, menstrual”) or a back-formation from mestruale (“menstrual (relational)”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mēta. Doublet of meda.
From Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).
From Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).

parole.significato: a shed, typical of Tuscany, where chestnuts are dried up

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin meteorum (likely through the plural meteora; the singular would've likely yielded meteoro), from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron).
Borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).
From Latin metopa, from Ancient Greek μετόπη (metópē), from μετά (metá, “meta-”) + ὀπή (opḗ, “hole”).
From Latin metricus, from Ancient Greek μετρικός (metrikós), from μέτρον (métron).
From Latin metrum (“a measure”), from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).

parole.significato: to put, to place, to lay, to set
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with French mettre, Spanish meter, Occitan metre, and English mission.
From Latin mediānus, whence also Italian mediano (a borrowed doublet).
From mezza (“half; mid”) + notte (“night”), or directly from Latin mediam noctem.
Inherited from Latin media hebdomas (literally “half week”), compare Dalmatian misedma, Old High German mittawehha. By surface analysis, mezza + edima.
From Latin medius, whence also Italian medio (a borrowed doublet).
Inherited from Latin mītius (“rather/too mild, mellow”, comparative neuter singular of mītis (“mild”)).
From busto, through a semantic shift from Latin būstum (“burial mound”, “tomb”). By surface analysis, mezzo- (“half-”) + busto (“torso”, “trunk”).
From mezzo + dì, or directly from Latin mediam diem. Compare French midi, Catalan migdia, Occitan mieidia, Portuguese meio-dia, Spanish mediodía, Romanian miazăzi.

Inherited from Latin mīca, from Proto-Italic *smīkā, from Proto-Indo-European *smeyg- (“small, thin, delicate”). Cognate in particular with Old French mie, with whom it shares the semantic broadening from a (bread)crumb to "not (at all), few".
Borrowed from Latin mīca, the same source as the above.
Formed from the root of Latin mīca, with the suffix -ella, or borrowed from New Latin micella.
From Latin Mycēnaeus, from Ancient Greek Μυκηναῖος (Mukēnaîos).

parole.significato: pussy, pussy-cat, puss (affectionate term for a cat)
parole.testo: Probably derived from mucio, a form used in southern italian dialects, from Latin mūsiō (“cat”). Isidore of Seville quotes mūsiō as the correct form and cattus as the popular (vulgar) form in his Etymologiæ. The standard pronunciation is due to spelling, while central dialects preserve the etymologi
From New Latin microscopium, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “I look at”).
From midolla, from Latin medulla, or through a Vulgar Latin form *medullum. Compare Spanish meollo, Portuguese miolo, Catalan moll, Sicilian miduḍḍa.
From Latin metere, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to mow, reap”).

parole.significato: any of several forms of Neapolitan cake made from millet or maize flour
thousand, about a thousand, about one thousand
the Italian mile, a traditional unit of length derived from the Roman mile
parole.testo: Back-formation from the plural miglia, from Latin mīlia n pl (“thousand”) in the phrase mīlia passuum (“thousand paces”). Doublet of mille.
Inherited from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Inherited from Latin meliōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *mélyōs, from *mel- (“strong, big”).
Borrowed from Latin mīlliāre < mīlliārius < mīlle.

parole.significato: to serve as a soldier, to militate

parole.testo: From Latin mīlitia. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from Polish milicja.
From Latin mīlle, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”). Doublet of miglio.
Borrowed from Latin millennium. Re-analyzable as mille + -ennio.
From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μιμικός (mimikós).
From Latin minācia (“threat”), a noun based on mināx (“threatening”).
From minestrare (“to serve, prepare (as in soup)”), from Latin ministrāre.
Inherited from Latin minūtia. Doublet of minuzza (inherited) and minuzia (borrowed).

parole.significato: an unintelligent or mentally challenged person
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin minus habēns (literally “that has less, having less”).
From Latin minūtus. Doublet of menu.
Borrowed from Latin minūtia. Doublet of minugia (inherited).
From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin mīrābilia, neuter plural form of the adjective mīrābilis (“wonderful, marvelous”). Doublet of meraviglia.
Borrowed from Latin mīrāculum, from mīror.

parole.significato: to aim, to take aim, to sight, to point

parole.testo: From Latin myrrha (also murra), from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), of Semitic origin.
From Latin myrrhis, from Ancient Greek μυρρίς (murrhís), from μύρρᾱ (múrrhā).
From Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos).

parole.significato: used to express negation; not, un-
parole.testo: Probably a confluence of Latin minus and Old High German missa-.
Borrowed from Latin miserābilis, derived from miseror (“to have pity”). By surface analysis, misero + -abile. Doublet of miserevole.
From misero, from Latin miserum. By surface analysis, misera (“unhappy”, “bleak”) + -mente (“-ly”, adverbial derivational suffix)
Borrowed from Latin miserēre (literally “have mercy!”), second-person singular active imperative form of miseror.
Borrowed from Latin miserābilis, partially remodelled with the suffix -evole. Doublet of miserabile.
Borrowed from Latin miseria (“misery”). By surface analysis, mìsero + -èria.
From Latin miserum, of uncertain origin. Possibly a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin mystagōgus, from Ancient Greek μυσταγωγός (mustagōgós).
From Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós).

parole.significato: mixture, mix, something made by combining multiple elements
mitre (covering for the head worn by church dignitaries)
parole.testo: From Latin mitra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”).
From Latin mittentem, present active participle of mittō.
Inherited from Latin modo (“recently, just now”) or Latin mox (“soon”), possibly a merger of both.
From Latin mōbilia, neuter plural form of mōbilis (“movable”).
From Latin moderāre, an alternative form of moderor, moderārī (“moderate, mitigate, restrain”).

parole.significato: modest, unpretentious, plain, unassuming, reserved, humble

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin modificāre (“to limit; to control, regulate”).
From Latin modus, from Proto-Indo-European *modós, derived from the root *med- (“to measure”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin modus operandī (literally “method of working”).
From Latin modius. Doublet of mozzo.
Inherited from Latin mulier (nominative). The alternative forms reflect the Latin accusative mulierem.
Inherited from Latin mola, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin mulcēre, with change of conjugation.
Inherited from Latin mollitia. Doublet of mollizia, which was borrowed. By surface analysis, molle + -ezza.

parole.significato: multiplicand (number that is to be multiplied by another)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin multiplicandus, gerundive of multiplicō (“to increase; to multiply”).
Learned borrowing from Latin multiplicātor. By surface analysis, moltiplicare + -tore.

parole.significato: much, very much, a lot (with verbs)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Portuguese muito, Romanian mult, Catalan molt.
From Latin monasterium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion).
From Latin monaulos, from Ancient Greek μόναυλος (mónaulos).
From Latin monēta. Compare Spanish moneda and Portuguese moeda.
Borrowed from Latin monētārius (“of or belonging to the mint”).
Learned borrowing from Latin monitōrem, derived from moneō (“to advise”). The “advisor” meaning is influenced by English monitor, and the “informer” one by French moniteur.

parole.significato: a variety of grape, cultivated in the Marche, Abruzzi and Apulia; a red wine made from these grapes (more usually uncap…
parole.testo: monte + pulciano, personal name, from dialectal Pulsa, from Latin publicianus, variant of publicius, from publicus and ultimately Etruscan.
From Latin monumentum, possibly a borrowing.
From Latin mōrālis, derived from mōs (“custom, way; law”).

Inherited from Latin morbidum (“sick”), from Latin morbus (“disease, illness”); as sickness makes one feeble, in Italo-Romance the meaning evolved into “limp, flabby”, and thence into “tender”, “delicate”.

parole.significato: pungent (having a sharp and stiff point)
as husband and wife; in a manner similar to a common-law marriage

parole.testo: From Latin mormyr, itself from Ancient Greek μορμύρος (mormúros).
Inherited from Latin mōrus (“black mulberry tree”), from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
From a diminutive of Latin murtatum (“sausage seasoned with myrtle berries”), from myrtatum, from myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos).

parole.significato: mortar (small vessel used to grind things)

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mortem, from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).

parole.significato: One person's survival or success comes at the expense of another's demise or failure.
parole.testo: Literally, “your death, my life”. Calque of Latin mors tua vita mea.

Borrowed from Latin mortifer, mortiferus, derived from mors (“death”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying”), originally a calque of Ancient Greek θᾰνᾰτηφόρος (thănătēphóros, “deadly, lethal”, literally “death-bearing”). By surface analysis, morte + -ifero.
From Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-. Compare Spanish mosca.

parole.significato: a traditional diamond-shaped Christmas sweet, from Naples, made with nuts
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin mustaceus (“wedding cake”), from mustum (“must”), because it was prepared from flour mixed with must.
From Latin mustum, neuter of mustus (“fresh, young", and, of wine, "unfermented”), from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”). Cognate with Sicilian mustu.
Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre (“to show”). Cognate with Spanish mostrar, Occitan muishar and French montrer.
From the older form monstro, from Latin mōnstrum.

Inherited from Latin maltha (“mineral pitch”). The original [ɫ] appears to have vocalized to [u̯] in pre-literary Tuscan, with the resulting [au̯] regularly yielding [ɔ], as in Latin aurum (“gold”) > Italian òro. Doublet of malta. Less probably of Germanic origin, related to English mud.

parole.significato: motor, motory, motive, propelling, driving, moving

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin muttum (“mutter”). Compare Catalan and French mot (“word”).
From Latin modium. Doublet of moggio.
Borrowed from Latin mūcus. Compare moccio, moccolo.
Inherited from Latin mūgilāre. See also mugolare.
Inherited from Latin mūgīre, from Proto-Indo-European *mug-, *mūg-, of onomatopoeic origin.
From the past participle of muggire, or from Latin mūgītus.
Borrowed from Latin muliebris, derived from mulier.
Learned borrowing from Latin mulsum, substantivization of the neuter form of mulsus (“mixed with honey”).

parole.significato: fine (a fee levied as punishment for breaking the law)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin multāre. By surface analysis, multa + -are.
From Latin multicolōrem. By surface analysis, multi- (“many”, “multi-”) + colore (“color”).
From Latin multifōrmis, calque of Ancient Greek πολύμορφος (polúmorphos). By surface analysis, multi- (“many”, “multi-”, multiplying prefix) + -forme (“form”, “shape”).

parole.significato: that wishes for (too) many things; inconstant, fickle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin multivolus, derived from multi- + the root of volō (“to want”).
Borrowed from Latin mūnerāre (“to present, reward”), derived from mūnus (“service, gift”).
From Latin mūnificentia, derived from mūnificēns (“bountiful”).

parole.significato: to fortify or equip something with something

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūnus (“service, gift”), from Proto-Italic *moinos (“service”), from Proto-Indo-European *moynós, derived from the root *mey- (“to change, swap”).
Borrowed from Latin mūnusculum, diminutive of mūnus (“gift; service”).
From Late Latin mūrālia, from Latin mūrālis. By surface analysis, muro (“wall”) + -aglia.

parole.significato: of or relating to a wall; on, or in, or against a wall
parole.testo: From muro (“wall”) + -ale (“-al”), or borrowed from Latin mūrālis; first attested 16th century.
From Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).
Derived from Latin mūsa/Mūsa, from Ancient Greek μοῦσα (moûsa)/Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

parole.significato: Muse-leading, used as an epithet for the gods Apollo and Hercules
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Mūsagetēs, from Doric Greek Μουσαγέτης (Mousagétēs), from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”) + Doric Greek ἀγέτης (agétēs, “leader”), literally “leader of the Muses”.

From Latin mūscus, probably through a diminutive Vulgar Latin root *mūsclus, from syncopation of an earlier *mūsculus. Compare Romanian mușchi, Friulian muscli. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mus-.
From muscolo + -oso, or from Latin musculōsus.
Probably borrowed from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “of a Muse”).
Probably from Provençal mus 'hair', derived from Latin mus (“mouse”).
From Latin mūtandae, from mūtandus (“which is to be changed”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin mūtātiōnem (“change, alteration”), derived from mūtō (“to change”).

parole.significato: to give or receive (money) as a loan
a decorative shelf protruding from an entablature
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūtulus. Compare mucchio, possibly an inherited doublet.
From Latin mūtuum (“loan”), from a noun use of the neuter form of mūtuus (“lent”, “borrowed”).
From Latin naias, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás, “naiad”), from νάειν (náein, “to flow”).
From Latin nānus, from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos).

parole.significato: Neapolitan (of, from or relating to the city of Naples, capital and largest city of Campania, Italy, or the surrounding…
parole.testo: From Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis (“Naples”), from Ancient Greek Νεᾱ́πολῐς (Neā́polĭs, literally “new city”).
From Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).

parole.significato: spikenard (plant or oil extracted from it)

From Latin nārrātīvus, from nārrō (“to narrate”).

From Latin nātīvus. Doublet of naïf.
From Latin nātus, from earlier gnātus, from Proto-Italic *gnātos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁tós (“begotten, produced”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, give birth”).

parole.significato: any snake of the Natrix taxonomic genus

Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Borrowed from Latin nauticus, from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós), derived from ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”).
From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (nautílos, “nautilus, sailor”).
From Latin nāvālis, derived from nāvis (“boat”).
From Latin nāvem, from Proto-Italic *naus ~ *nāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us, derived from the root *(s)neh₂- (“to swim, float”).

parole.significato: to sail, to go to sea

From Latin Nāzaraeus, alternative form of Nāzīraeus, from Ancient Greek Ναζωραῖος (Nazōraîos).

parole.significato: Nazianzen (of, from or relating to Nazianzus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nazianzēnus (“Nazianzen, of Nazianzus”). By surface analysis, Nazianzo (“Nazianzus”) + -eno (“pertaining to”).
From Latin inde (“thence, from that place; from that person, of them”). Compare French en (adverb, pronoun).

From Latin nebris, from Ancient Greek νεβρίς (nebrís), earlier νεβρός (nebrós, “fawn”).
Borrowed from Latin nebula. Doublet of nebbia, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin nebulōsus. Cognate to Italian nebbioso, which is however not a borrowing but an Italian formation.

Borrowed from Latin negātiōnem. By surface analysis, negare (“deny”) + -zione (“-tion”).

Borrowed from Latin negligentem, variant of neglegens.
Borrowed from Latin negligentia, variant of neglegentia.

parole.significato: to neglect to do something, neglect to take something into consideration

From negozio + -are or from Latin negōtiārī, possibly a semi-learned term. First attested 14th century.

Borrowed from Latin negōtium, possibly a semi-learned term. First attested 14th century.

From Latin necromantīa (with influence from negro), from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía).
Inherited from Latin nimbus. Doublet of nimbo.
From Latin inimīcus, with the loss of the first syllable.

From Latin nēpenthes, from Ancient Greek νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”) (neuter), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”).
Borrowed from Latin nēquitia, derived from nēquam (“worthless”).
Inherited from Latin nervus. Doublet of nervo.

From Latin nervus. Doublet of nerbo.
Inherited from Latin mespilum, which borrowed it from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon). For the unexpected /o/ in the second syllable of nespolo, compare -evole.

From Latin nē (“not”) + ipse (emphatic, literally “himself”) + ūnus (“one”), by surface analysis “not even one”. Cognate with Neapolitan nisciuno, Sardinian nisciunu, Friulian nissun, Ligurian nisciǜn, and Old French neisune. Compare Spanish ninguno and Romanian niciun.
From Latin nectar (genitive nectaris), from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).
From netto (“clear”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix) or directly from Latin nitidāre.
From Latin nectareus, from Ancient Greek νεκτάρεος (nektáreos). By surface analysis, nettare (“nectar”) + -eo (“-y”, suffix denoting the source of an attribute).
Borrowed from Latin Neptūnius, derived from Neptūnus.
Inherited from Latin nivem, from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs. Compare Portuguese neve, Spanish nieve.
Learned borrowing from Latin naevus, from earlier gnaevus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁iwós (“native”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget”). Doublet of neo.
Inherited from Latin nivōsus. By surface analysis, neve (“snow”) + -oso (“-y, -ous”).

parole.significato: Nivôse (the fourth month of the French Republican Calendar)
parole.testo: Taken from Latin nivōsus (“snowy”), as a calque of French nivôse.
Alteration of Latin onychinus (“made of onyx”), from onyx (“onyx”).
Inherited from Latin nīdus, from Proto-Italic *nizdos (“nest”), from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”). Compare French nid, Spanish nido, Portuguese ninho.

parole.significato: the smell of burning animals, nidor

parole.testo: From an earlier neente, either from Latin ne gentem (“no person, no one”), nec entem, ne entem, or ne inde. Borrowed from Latin nigritia. Doublet of nerezza, which was inherited.
From Latin nīlōticus, from Ancient Greek Νειλωτικός (Neilōtikós).
Borrowed from Latin nimbus (“cloud, halo”). Doublet of nembo.
Learned borrowing from Latin nimius (“excessive”), derived from nimis (“too much, excessively”).
From Latin nympha or nymphe (“nymph”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “young woman, nymph”).
From Latin nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Compare French neveu, Romanian nepot, Catalan and Occitan nebot, Sicilian niputi and Persian نوه.
Borrowed from Latin nīsus, alternative form of nīxus (“strain”, noun), derived from nītor (“to press forward, to advance”).
Borrowed from Latin nitidus. Doublet of the inherited netto.
Borrowed from Latin nōbilitāre. By surface analysis, nobile (“noble”) + -itare.
From Old Italian nobilità, nobilitade, nobilitate, from Latin nōbilitātem (“fame; nobility”).
Inherited from Latin nauclērus, itself from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).

Probably derived from Latin nucleus (perhaps the variant form nuculeus), from nux (“nut”), or from the diminutive nucleolus; alternatively from nuceu(m), nuceus (“of nuts”), with influence from nocciola. Compare Sicilian nòzzulu.
Inherited from Latin nucem. Cognate with Sicilian nuci.
Inherited from Latin nocentem (“harmful; guilty”), present active participle of noceō (“to harm, damage”), whence Italian nuocere.
From Latin nucētum. Compare Romanian nucet and Sicilian nucitu.
Inherited from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin nōluntātem (“unwillingness”), derived from nōlō (“to be unwilling, to not want”) on the example of vōluntās (“will; desire”).
Borrowed from Latin nōmenclātūra (“a calling by name, list of names”). Doublet of nomenklatura.

parole.significato: of or relating to the Sabine city Nomentum, modern day Mentana

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nōminātīvus, derived from nōminō (“to name, give name to”).
From Latin nōminātīvus [cāsus], calque of ὀνομαστική [πτῶσις] (onomastikḗ [ptôsis]).
Borrowed from Latin nominātiōnem. By surface analysis, nominare + -zione.

parole.significato: the very best, the ne plus ultra
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin nōn plūs ultra.
Borrowed from Latin nōnāgēsimus, derived from nōnāgintā (“ninety”).
Inherited from Latin nōnnūllā, neuter plural (collective) of Latin nōnnūllus, itself from nōn (“not”) + nūllus (“no one, no, not any”).

parole.significato: related to a damage or harm; only used in azione nossale
parole.testo: From Latin noxālis, derived from noxa (“harm”, “damage”).
Inherited from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Latin nocturnus, from noctū (“by night”), from nox (“night”), whence also Italian notte, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Borrowed from Latin novātiōnem (“a renewing, renovation”), from novō, from novus (“new”).
From Latin novem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Portuguese nove, Spanish nueve.
Inherited from Latin numerus (via old intermediary forms *nomero > *nombero > *nobero), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”). Doublet of numero, a borrowing.
From earlier novitade, novitate, from Latin novitātem (“newness, novelty”).
Learned borrowing from Latin nūbēcula, diminutive of nūbēs (“cloud”).

parole.significato: one who is about to get married
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūbendus, gerundive of nūbō (“to marry”).
Inherited from Latin nūlla, feminine singular and neuter plural (collective) of nūllus.

parole.significato: a god, particularly that of Greco-Roman mythology

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerāre. Compare noverare, an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin numerus, whence also Italian novero (an inherited doublet).
Borrowed from Latin numerōsus. By surface analysis, numero + -oso. Compare novero.
Inherited from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, from the root *new-.
Borrowed from Latin nūtantem, present active participle of nūtō (“to nod”).
Latinized form of archaic versions, from Latin nūtrīcem.
Borrowed from Latin nūtrientem, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).

Inherited from Latin nūbilātus. By surface analysis, nuvola + -ato. Compare Spanish and Portuguese nublado, Galician nubrado, Asturian nubláu, Friulian nulât.
From Latin nūbilus (“cloudy”). For the unexpected /o/ in the second syllable, compare -evole.

parole.significato: The thirteenth letter of the Italian alphabet, called o and written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: From Latin ō (the name of the letter O).
From Latin opprobrium (“reproach; scandal”), derived from opprobrō (“to reproach, taunt”).
From Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”).
Borrowed from Latin obēsitātem, from obēsus (“fat”) (compare obeso).
From Latin obēsus, derived from obedō (“to devour”).
From Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“throw against”), from ob (“against”) + iaciō (“throw”).

parole.significato: to objurgate, to deplore, to condemn solemnly, to blame

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oblīviōnem, form of oblīviō, derived from oblīviscor (“to forget”).
Borrowed from Latin obtēctus (“covered”), perfect passive participle of obtegō.

Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem, whence also Italian cagione (an inherited doublet).
Borrowed from Latin occidentem, present participle of occidō (“to fall down; pass away”), in reference to the setting of the Sun.

parole.significato: Old Italian form of uccidere (“to kill”)
parole.testo: From Latin occidō (“to fall down, perish”).
Present participle of occorrere. From Latin occurrentem.

parole.significato: must; to need; to be necessary

parole.testo: From Latin occultus, past participle form of occulō (“to hide, conceal”).

parole.significato: to occupy, take over, squat in
occupation (the act of occupying and the state of being occupied)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōceanus, from the name of the deity Ōceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεᾰνός (Ōkeănós).
Borrowed from Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”).
Borrowed from Latin oculus (“eye”). Doublet of occhio, which was inherited.
From Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin odium (“hate”), whence also uggia, inherited through Vulgar Latin.
Borrowed from Latin odiōsus, derived from odium (“hatred”).

parole.significato: to smell (an odor, a flower, etc.), to perceive with the sense of smell
parole.testo: From Latin odōrāre (“to perfume, make fragrant”), derived from odor (“smell”).

parole.significato: smell, odour, odor, aroma, fragrance, scent
parole.testo: From Latin odōrem, from an archaic form odōs, from Proto-Italic *odōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃édos, derived from the root *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Doublet of aulore and olore.
Borrowed from Latin odōriferum, form of odōrifer, derived from odor (“smell”). By surface analysis, odore + -ifero.

parole.significato: the collective means aimed at preventing invasion of domicile or property (like, e.g., barbed wire)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin offendicula, plural of offendiculum (“obstacle, hindrance”), derived from offendō.
Borrowed from Latin officīna. Doublet of fucina, which was inherited.
Latin ungula. Superseded by Tuscan unghia.

Inherited from Old Italian onne~onni (with /ˈɔ-/ per the Latin etymon), from Latin omnis. The development of palatalized /-ɲ-/ and closed /ˈo-/, already attested in the thirteenth century (ógne, later ógni), are due to the word being frequently unstressed. Variants with /ˈɔ-/ still survive in much o
From Latin olentem, form of olēns, present active participle of oleō (“to smell, emit an odor”).
From Latin olfactus, derived from olfaciō (“to smell, scent”).
From Latin olfactōrius, from olfactus, present participle of olfaciō (“to sniff”), from oleō + faciō.
From Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).
From Latin olēre (with a later change in a conjugation), from an earlier form olō, from Proto-Italic *odō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell”). Doublet of aulire.
From Latin ulmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).
Inherited from Latin ultra, from ulter. Cognate with French outre, from Old French oltre.
Inherited from Latin umbilīcus. Compare Sicilian viḍḍicu.
From Latin umbra, probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-.
From Latin umbrōsus, from umbra; by surface analysis, ombra + -oso.
From Latin humerus, umerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃émsos (“shoulder”).
Adapted from Latin omittere, to Italian mettere.
From the stem homin- of Latin homō (“man”) + -zione (“-tion”).
Borrowed from Latin ōminōsus, derived from ōmen (“omen”).
Learned borrowing from Latin onagrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass, donkey”) + ᾰ̓́γρῐος (ắgrĭos, “wild”).
From Latin unda, from nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).
Learned borrowing from Latin undāre (“to rise in waves”), derived from unda (“wave”).
From Latin undātus, perfect passive participle of undō (“to rise in waves”), derived from unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: that resounds with the roar of the waves; undisonant

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃énh₂os, from the root *h₃enh₂- (“to onerate, charge”).
From Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυχος (ónukhos), from ὄνυξ (ónux, “(finger)nail”).
From Latin oniscus, from Ancient Greek ὀνισκος (oniskos), diminutive of ὄνος (ónos, “donkey, ass”).
Borrowed from Latin omnipotentem. By surface analysis, onni- (“omni-, all-”) + potente (“powerful, mighty”).
From Latin onōnis, from Ancient Greek ὀνωνίς (onōnís).
Borrowed from Latin honōrābilis, from honor + -ābilis. Doublet of onorevole.

parole.significato: to honour/honor, to pay tribute to

Borrowed from Latin honōrābilis, remodelled with the suffix -evole. Doublet of onorabile.
From Latin onustus (“burdened”, “loaded”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃enh₂ostos, from the root *h₃enh₂- (“to onerate, charge”).

parole.significato: opaque (allowing little light to pass through)
parole.testo: (Possibly borrowed) from Latin opācus (“shaded, shady, dark”), itself of unknown origin.
From Latin operārius. By surface analysis, from operare + -aio
Borrowed from Latin operātōrem. By surface analysis, operare + -tore.

parole.significato: to opine, to think, to deem

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).

parole.significato: to put forward, raise (points of view, arguments)
opportune, timely, suitable, fit, appropriate, right

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin opus. Doublet of the inherited Old Italian uopo.

parole.significato: hour (a unit of time of one twenty-fourth of a day (sixty minutes))
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “hour”).
Derived from Latin hōrā, ablative case of hōra (“hour”). Compare Old French ore, Spanish ahora and Portuguese agora.
Inherited from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”). Doublet of the borrowing aura.
Inherited from Latin aurifex. Doublet of orefice.
Borrowed from Latin ōrāre (“to orate; to plead; to pray”), derived from ōs (“mouth”).
From Latin aurātus, perfect passive participle of aurō (“to gild”), derived from aurum (“gold”).
Inherited from Latin laurī bacca (“laurel berry”), with deglutination of the l-, perceived as an article.
Learned borrowing from Latin orbāre, derived from orbus (“deprived”).

From orcio + -olo (diminutive), or from Latin urceolus.
From Latin Orcus (“god of the underworld”), orcus.

From Latin orgia, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia).
From Latin ōricula (“a little ear”), a diminutive of auris (“ear”).

From Latin orientem (possibly a borrowing), accusative form of oriēns, present participle of orior (“to rise, get up”), in reference to the rising of the Sun. Early Christian maps were "oriented" with the direction to Jerusalem always at the top.
From Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὀρίγανον (oríganon).
Inherited from Latin ūrīnārī. By surface analysis, orina (“urine”) + -are.

parole.significato: native (of a place, especially native of Italy but living abroad)
parole.testo: Borrowed fom Latin oriundus (“descended from”), from orior (“to rise, originate”).
Borrowed from Latin horizontem, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
From Latin ōrnāmentum (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from ōrnō (“to equip, adorn”).
From Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-.

parole.significato: forms terms related to the mouth; oral

From Latin hōrologium, from Koine Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).
From Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos).

From Latin horrēre (“to dread ← to tremble, shiver ← to stand erect, stand on end”), from Proto-Italic *horzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥séh₁(ye)ti, derived from the root *ǵʰers- (“stiff”).
From Latin horrōrem, from Proto-Italic *horzōs, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰórsōs, derived from the root *ǵʰers- (“stiff; surprised”).
From Latin urtīca. Compare Sicilian ardìcula.

Borrowed from Latin ōsculum, diminutive of ōs (“mouth”).
Borrowed from Latin obscūritātem. By surface analysis, oscuro (“dark”) + -ità (“-ity”).

Borrowed from Latin ossārium, alternative form of ossuārium (“ossuary”). By surface analysis, osso (“bone”) + -ario.
Borrowed from Latin observandus, gerundive of observō (“to heed, to respect”).

From Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan, French, and Romanian os; Portuguese osso; Corsican, Sardinian, and Sicilian ossu; Spanish hueso.

parole.significato: obstacle (something that impedes, stands in the way of, or holds up progress)
to stand in the way of, to hinder, to oppose
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin obstāre. In modern usage, only used with nulla (“nothing”) as subject, from which also the substantive nullaosta.

parole.significato: army or host, especially that of the enemy
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hostem (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“guest, stranger”).

parole.significato: that can be shown or exhibited; displayable

From Latin hostīlis, derived from hostis (“enemy”).

From Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).

parole.significato: to obtain, to achieve, to gain (something desired)

parole.significato: very good, very fine, excellent, perfect, splendid

to multiply by eight, to octuple

From Latin pāgānus (“rural; villager”), derived from pāgus (“area outside of a city; countryside”).

parole.significato: to pay (money, a bill, the rent, etc.)

Back-formation as a masculine noun from the plural paia, from Latin paria (“even, equal”, neuter plural of pār). Cognate with Sicilian paru.
From Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome. Doublet of palazzo.
Inherited from Latin pālāre. By surface analysis, palo + -are.

Inherited from Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome. Cognate to English palace, French palais, Spanish palacio, Portuguese paço, palácio, see more at palātium.

parole.significato: Palermitan (of, from or relating to the city of Palermo, Sicily, Italy)

Probably borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).
From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).

Borrowed from Latin Palladius, from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιος (Palládios), derived from Παλλάς (Pallás), epithet of the goddess Athena.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Palladium, from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), derived from Παλλάς (Pallás) (see Etymology 1).

From Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis).

From Latin parāre, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).

From Latin parasītus, from Ancient Greek παράσῑτος (parásītos, “person who eats at the table of another”). Ending reshaped by erroneous analogy with the suffix -ita, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).

From Latin pardus, from Ancient Greek παρδός (pardós).

From Latin parvulus, diminutive of parvus.

parole.significato: parietal (of or pertaining to the wall of a body part or to the parietal bone)

parole.testo: Uncertain; according to the OED, possibly related to Latin pilus (“hair”), but there are phonetic difficulties. From pelo + -are or from Latin pilāre (“to deprive of hair”).
From Latin Pelasgicus, from Ancient Greek Πελασγικός (Pelasgikós), derived from Πελασγίᾱ (Pelasgíā).
