From Latin scarabaeus, from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”).
Inherited from Latin scheda, from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”). Doublet of scheda.
Inherited from Latin scelerāre (“to defile”), derived from scelus (“evil deed”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scelus, from Proto-Indo-European *skélos, derived from the root *(s)kel- (“bent, crooked”). Cognate with Greek σκέλος (skélos, “leg”).

Inherited from Latin simplus (“simple”), under the influence of scemo (“silly”). However, for other examples of initial s- palatalized to sci-, see scimmia, scialiva, sciringa (doublet of siringa). Compare the synonym semplice.
Inherited from Latin exemplum (“warning example, penalty”). Doublet of esempio. Compare Sicilian scempru.
Borrowed from Latin scēna, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

parole.significato: to go (all the way) down, come (all the way) down (the stairs)
parole.testo: From a reduction of the prefix in discendere, from Latin dēscendere.
From Latin secernō (“to distinguish, to discern”), related to Provençal eissernir.
Inherited from Latin excerpere (“to choose, select”), with a change in conjugation.
From Latin scheda (“piece of paper”), from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”). Doublet of sceda.

parole.significato: splinter, shiver, shrapnel, chip, spell, spelk, shard
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin schidia, from Ancient Greek σχίδια (skhídia).

parole.significato: outline, schema, layout, diagram, plan, draft, project, arrangement
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin schema, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).

parole.significato: to make noise, to clamour, to din (of people)
parole.testo: From Latin exclamāre, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *ex-clamitiāre. Compare esclamare, which was borrowed.

Deverbal from schiamazzare + -o. Alternatively, possibly corresponds to Latin exclāmatiō (whence also the borrowing esclamazione, from the accusative form), with the verb derived from the noun instead. Compare also Old French esclamasse.
Perhaps from Latin explantāre or from a blend of schiattare (“to burst”) and spiantare (“to ruin”).
See scoppio (“explosion”), of onomatopoeic origin. Alternatively from Latin stloppus (“sound of a slap”).
Inherited from Latin exclūdere. By surface analysis, s- + chiudere. Compare the borrowed doublet escludere.
From Latin exa(u)gurātus, perfect passive participle of exaugurō (“to desecrate, make profane, exaugurate”), from ex- + augurō.

parole.significato: to be extravagant; to spend money like water
parole.testo: From Latin exhalāre, from ex- (“out”) + halō (“to breathe”). Cognate with Sicilian scialari.

Inherited from Latin saliva, probably with influence of the prefix ex-, cf. sceverare. However, it would be unusual for this prefix to be attached to a noun. For more examples of initial s- palatalized to sci-, see scimmia, scempio, sciringa (doublet of siringa).
Inherited from Latin exāmen. Compare the borrowed doublet esame.
Borrowed from Latin scyphus (“cup”), from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).
Inherited from Latin scilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla).

From earlier scimia, Latin sīmia, from Ancient Greek σῑμός (sīmós, “snub-nosed”). For more examples of initial s- palatalized to sci-, see scialiva, scempio, sciringa (doublet of siringa). Compare Sicilian scìmia.
From Latin sīmius, from Ancient Greek σῑμός (sīmós, “snub-nosed”).
From Latin scincos, from Ancient Greek σκίγγος (skíngos), σκίγκος (skínkos).
From Latin scindere, from Proto-Italic *skindō, from Proto-Indo-European *skinédti (“to be cutting off”), derived from the root *skeyd- (“to split”).

parole.significato: to scintillate, to sparkle, to glitter

parole.testo: Perhaps from Latin exsuccus (“sapless, lifeless”), from ex- + succus (“juice, moisture”) (compare exsūcō).

parole.significato: to melt, to liquify, to dissolve, to thaw
parole.testo: From Latin exsolvere (“to unloose, release, free; to unbind, untie, undo”). Compare Sicilian sciògghiri.
From Latin dissipāre or Latin *exsipāre. See also sciupare.
From Latin scirros, from Ancient Greek σκῖρος (skîros).
Borrowed from Latin scissile(m), accusative form of scissilis.

parole.significato: synonym of bastonatura, clubbing, caning, beating, especially (historical) the Scytalismus, the clubbing of wealthy Arg…
parole.testo: From Latin scytalismus, from Ancient Greek σκυταλισμός (skutalismós), from σκυτάλη (skutálē) or σκύταλον (skútalon) + -ισμός (-ismós).
The word is probably of onomatopoeic origin. From Latin exsībilāre. . Also possibly a portmanteau of sci (“ski”) + volare (“to fly”), which is perhaps a folk etymology.
From earlier *scotella, from Latin scutella, diminutive of scutra.
Inherited from Latin spolia, plural of spolium (“stripped-off animal skin or hide”), with influence from scaglia (“scale”) or scorza (“rind”).
Borrowed from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολαστικός (skholastikós).
From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).
From Latin scolopendra, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra).
From Latin sculpere (“to carve, chisel”), whence also sculpt, sculpture.

parole.significato: to smash to pieces, to shatter (by shaking violently)
parole.testo: From s- (intensifier) + conquassare, from Latin conquassāre (“to shake violently, to shatter”), from Latin quassāre (“to shake repeatedly”), whence also French casser (“to break”).

parole.significato: to copy or imitate badly or clumsily
parole.testo: From s- + copia (“copy”) + -azzare (pejorative suffix), from Latin cōpia (“abundance”).
From Latin scōpa (“branch of a plant”), whence also Italian scopa (“broom”). Compare Albanian shqopë (“heather”). See also scoviglio (“brush”).
Metathesized counterpart to schioppo (“gun”), from Latin stloppus (“slap”, with /tl/ > /kl/ > /kj/).
Borrowed from Latin scōpula, diminutive of scōpa (“broom”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek σκόπελος (skópelos). Doublet of scoglio.
From s- + (ri)cordare. Ultimately from Latin excors (“senseless”).
From Latin scorpaena, from Ancient Greek σκόρπαινα (skórpaina). Doublet of scorpena, a learned borrowing.
From Latin scōria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría).
From Latin scorpaena, from Ancient Greek σκόρπαινα (skórpaina). Doublet of scorfano.

parole.significato: to run, to flow, to stream, to glide, to slide

parole.testo: From Latin scortum (“skin, hide”), via scortea (“leather bag or garment”), nominalization of scorteus (“made of skin or leather”). Compare French écorce, Romanian scoarță, Sicilian scorcia.
From Latin cotinus, from Ancient Greek κότινος (kótinos).

parole.significato: overcooked, overdone (chiefly of pasta and rice)
parole.testo: From Latin excoctus, perfect passive participle of excoquō (“to boil; to melt”).
Borrowed from Latin scotia, from Ancient Greek σκοτῐ́ᾱ (skotĭ́ā, “dark, shadowy [hole]”).

parole.significato: discord that comes to disturb the harmony of a relationship; disagreement, friction, tiff
parole.testo: Uncertain, but possibly a borrowing, with apheresis, from Latin discrētiō (“difference”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scrība. Doublet of scrivano.
From scrivere + -acchiare, in this form matching Latin scrībere or scrība.

Derived from Latin scrīpta, noun use of the neuter plural form of scrīptus (“written”), perfect passive participle of scrībō (“to write”). By surface analysis, deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of scrivere.
Inherited from Latin scrīptus (“written”), perfect passive participle of scrībō (“to write”).
Inherited from Latin scriptum, noun use of the neuter form of scrīptus (“written”), perfect passive participle of scrībō (“to write”).
From Latin scrīptōrius, derived from scrīptus (“written”), perfect passive participle of scrībō (“to write”).

parole.significato: a unit of measure equivalent to 1/24 of an ounce
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scrūpulus (“sharp stone”, figuratively “anxiety, uneasiness”).

parole.significato: to scrutinize, to scan, to examine (to look or examine carefully to try to see or understand things that are not immedi…

parole.testo: From earlier *scuto, from Latin scūtum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skei- (“to cut, split”), an extension of *sek- (“to cut”).
From Latin sculptōrem. Cognate with Friulian scultôr, Lombard scultor, Piedmontese scultor.
Inherited from Latin schola. First attested in the 14th century. Compare Sicilian scola.
From Latin excussus, perfect passive participle of excutiō (“to shake off; to discard”).
From uncertain Vulgar Latin, likely from Latin resuere (“to unstitch”), from suere.
From Latin sī (“if”) or from Late Latin se(d), from Latin sī and quid ("what").
Borrowed from Latin sebaceus. By surface analysis, sebo + -aceo.
Borrowed from Latin sēbum. Compare the inherited doublet sego (older sevo).
Borrowed from Latin secāre. Compare the doublet segare (“to saw”).
From Latin siccāneus, derived from siccus.
From secco, from Latin siccus, from a Proto-Indo-European root *seyk-. By surface analysis, secco (“dry”) + -ezza (“-ness”, nominal derivational suffix).

parole.significato: bucket used to get water (from a well, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin situla. Compare secchio.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin saeculāris. The meanings related to religion started developing through the works of Christian authors.
From Latin secundus (“he who follows, second”), from sequor (“to follow”). Cognate with Sicilian sicunnu.
From Latin secundum (“after, behind, according to”, preposition and adverb).
From Latin sēcrēt(us) + Ancient Greek ἀγωγός (agōgós, “that leads”).
From Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
From earlier secare (merged with the borrowing), inherited from Latin secāre. Doublet of secare, a borrowing from Latin.

parole.significato: to mark, mark out, or tick
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin signāre. By surface analysis, segno + -are.
From Latin signum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”) or *sekʷ- (“to follow”).
Variant of sevo, from Latin sēbum, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out”). Cf. also sebo.
* adjective: From Latin sēcrētus (perfect passive participle of sēcērnō) * noun: From Latin sēcrētum (noun form of secretus)
From Latin sequāx (“following”). Cognate with Spanish secuaz and Portuguese sequaz.

parole.significato: flint (hard fine-grained quartz which generates sparks when struck)

parole.testo: From Latin selēnītēs, from Ancient Greek σεληνῑ́της (selēnī́tēs, “moonstone”), derived from σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”).
From Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
From Latin silva, from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *swel- (“beam, board, frame, threshold”).
From Latin silvāticus (with the variant form from Vulgar Latin salvāticus), from silva (“forest”). Compare French sauvage, Romanian sălbatic, Sicilian sarbaggiu. Doublet of selvaggio.
Inherited from Latin sēmen, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.
In sense 1, deverbal from sementare + -a. In sense 2, an alternative form of semente, from Latin sementem.

parole.significato: seed (all the seeds of a species destined to inseminate an area of land)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sēmentem. Compare Sicilian simenza.
From Latin semestris (“six months”), from sex (“six”) + mensis (“month”).
Inherited from Latin sēminātōrem. Morphologically, seminare + -tore.

parole.significato: semolina (coarse grains of hard wheat used to make pasta)
parole.testo: From Latin simila (“finest wheat flour”). For the unexpected /o/ in the second syllable, compare -evole.
Borrowed from Latin sempiternus, derived from semper (“always”).

Attested from ca. 1261. A cross of inherited sempice, semprice with Latin simplicem, from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”) + *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). Compare duplice, molteplice. Partial doublet of scempio.
Inherited from Latin semper; compare Catalan and Portuguese sempre, Spanish siempre.
From Latin sinapi, from Ancient Greek σίναπι (sínapi). Compare Sicilian sinapi.
Borrowed from Latin senem, from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”).
From Latin senēscentem (“ageing”, “decaying”), present active participle of senēscō (“to grow old”).
From Latin senecta, derived from senectus (“old”), derived from senex.
Borrowed from Latin senectūtem (“old age”), derived from senex (“old”).
From Latin senium (“feebleness, debility (of old age)”), derived from senex (“old”).
Inherited from Latin sinus (“fold, lap”). Compare French sein, Romansh sain, Romanian sân, Spanish seno, Persian سینه.
From Latin sine (“without”) conflated with absentia (“without, in the absence of”). Compare French sans.
Borrowed from Latin sentientem, present active participle of sentiō (“to feel, perceive”).
Probably borrowed from Latin sēparāre. Doublet of the inherited severare, older form of sceverare; compare also disceverare.
Borrowed from Latin separātiōnem. By surface analysis, separare + -zione.
From Latin sepulcrālis. By surface analysis, sepolcro + -ale.
Borrowed from Latin sequestrum (“depository”), derived from sequester (“mediator, trustee”).
From sereno (“clear, calm”), from Latin serenus (“calm”) or from the feminine past participle of serenare.
From Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sermōnem (“conversation; speech”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *serpes, from Latin serpēns, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.
Inherited from Latin serpentem, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.

parole.significato: to snake (to follow or move in a winding route)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin serpere (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Italic *serpō, from Proto-Indo-European *sérp-e-ti ~ *sérp-onti, thematic root present of *serp- (“to creep, crawl”). Cognate with Greek έρπω (érpo, “to crawl, creep”).

parole.significato: wild thyme (plant of the species Thymus serpyllum)

parole.testo: From Latin seranda (“which is to be bolted, fastened”), feminine future participle of serō.
From the present participle of servire; possibly corresponds to Latin servientem. Cf. also serviente.
From older servitude, servitute, from Latin servitūtem (“slavery, servitude”), from servus (“slave, servant”).
Borrowed from Latin servitium, from servus (“slave”). Compare Portuguese serviço, French service, Norman sèrvice, Sicilian sirbizzu, Spanish servicio.

parole.significato: servile (of or pertaining to a slave)
parole.testo: From Latin servus, from Proto-Indo-European *ser-wo- (“guardian”), or perhaps of Etruscan origin.
From Latin sīsamum, variant of sēsama, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon, “sesame seed”).
From Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).

parole.significato: sex (quality of being male or female)

parole.testo: From Latin sēta, from saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese seda.
Inherited from Latin saetacium or saetaceum, from saeta. Compare Spanish cedazo.
From Latin sitim, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“decay; destruction”), derived from the root *dʰgʷʰey- (“to decline; to perish”).

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Sezze
parole.testo: From Latin Sētīnus, from Sētia (“Sezze”) + -īnus (forming adjs.).
From Latin secta, probably from sectus (“cut off”), or alternatively from sequor, secutus.
From Latin septuāgintā, from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”).
Borrowed from Latin septem triōnēs (literally “the seven oxen”) or septentriō, septentriōnem which refers to one of the ancient names of the constellation of Ursa Major.

parole.significato: sectrix (curve which can be used to divide an arbitrary angle by any integer)
parole.testo: From Latin sectrīcem, feminine of sector (“one who cuts off”).

parole.significato: last (coming after all others in a succession)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin sētius (“later, slower”, adverb).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphaericus. By surface analysis, sfera + -ico.
Inherited from Latin exfricāre, variant of effricāre. By surface analysis, s- + fregare.

parole.significato: to tease, to taunt, to needle
parole.testo: From s- (intensive prefix) + a derivation of Latin fricāre (“to rub”).
From sfumare + -tura. Omitting several steps, from Latin fūmus. For the meaning development compare French nuance (from Latin nūbēs).

parole.significato: stool (low, such as a pouffe; or high, especially in a bar), footstool
parole.testo: From Latin scabellum, scabillum, diminutive of scamnum (“seat”).

parole.significato: to rumble, to suss, to suss out
parole.testo: Romanesco of uncertain origin. Probably from earlier scamare, maybe from Latin exquamare.
Possibly from Latin scorpius; if so, doublet of scorpione.
From Latin se (“him-, her-, it-, themselves”, reflexive third-person pronoun). Cognate with Spanish se and Portuguese se and si.

parole.significato: if you want peace, prepare for war
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin si vis pacem, para bellum.
Borrowed from Latin sībilāre, whence also Italian sobillare and zufolare (inherited doublets).
Borrowed from Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

parole.significato: sibylline (of or pertaining to a sibyl)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sibyllīnus, derived from Sibylla.
From Latin Sicānus, from Ancient Greek Σῑ̆κᾰνός (Sī̆kănós).
From Latin sīcārius (“murderer, assassin”), derived from sīca (“poniard, curved dagger”). By surface analysis, sica (“curved dagger”) + -ario (“-ary”).

parole.significato: one who informs the authorities of violations of the law
parole.testo: From Latin sȳcophanta (“informer, trickster”), from Ancient Greek σῡκοφάντης (sūkophántēs). The entomological sense is a semantic loan from translingual Calosoma sycophanta.
From Latin sycomorus, from Ancient Greek σῡκόμορος (sūkómoros): σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + μόρον (móron, “black mulberry”).
Inherited from Latin sēcūrus. Compare Spanish seguro.
Inherited from Latin sēcūritātem. By surface analysis, sicuro + -ità. First attested before 1294.
Borrowed from Latin sīdus (“constellation, star”, figuratively “season”).
From Latin sīphō from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”), of unknown ultimate origin.
Borrowed from Latin sigillāre. See also the doublet suggellare.
Borrowed from Latin sigillum. Doublet of the inherited suggello.
From earlier segnore, from Latin seniōrem, comparative form of senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos. Doublet of sire.

parole.significato: a human being with equine attributes (usually the ears and tail, sometimes the legs)
parole.testo: From Latin Sīlēnus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνός (Sīlēnós).
Borrowed from Latin silentem, present active participle of sileō (“to be silent”).

parole.significato: a domestic servant (usually a slave) who stood about his master, charged with seeing to it that no noise etc. disturbed…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin silentiārus, from silentium (“silence”), from sileō (“to be silent”).

parole.significato: silence!; shut up!; stop talking!; hush!
silent, voiceless, soundless, quiet, still, mute, noiseless, mum, taciturn

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin siliceus. Doublet of the inherited serizzo.
Borrowed from Latin syllaba, from Ancient Greek συλλαβή (sullabḗ).
From Latin silurus, borrowed from Ancient Greek σίλουρος (sílouros).
Borrowed from Latin silvestrem. Cf. salvastrella.
From Latin silvia, from silva (“wood, forest”).
Borrowed from Latin symbolum, from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon).
From Latin similitūdinem (“likeness, similitude; simile”). By surface analysis, simile + -itudine.
From Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).
Derived from Latin sīmus, from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós).

parole.significato: to simulate, to fake, to feign, to pretend
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin simulāre. Doublet of somigliare.
From Latin simulātiōnem. By surface analysis, simulare + -zione.
Borrowed from Latin sincēritātem. By surface analysis, sincero + -ità.
Learned borrowing from Latin sincērus (“pure, genuine”).
From Latin sindon, from Ancient Greek σινδών (sindṓn).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin sine diē (literally “without a day”).
Borrowed from Latin symphōnia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). Doublet of zampogna.
Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin singulāris. By surface analysis, singolo + -are. Doublet of cinghiale.
Learned borrowing from Latin singultus. Compare the inherited doublet singhiozzo.
Learned borrowing from Latin sinister. Doublet of sinestro.
Borrowed from Latin siparium, from Ancient Greek σίπαρος (síparos).
Borrowed from Latin Syriăcus, from Ancient Greek Συριακός (Suriakós), from Συρία (Suría).
Learned borrowing from Latin sitīre (“to thirst”), derived from sitis (“thirst”, noun).
From Latin situs (“laid, placed”), perfect passive participle of sinō (“to put, lay”), from Proto-Indo-European *si-n-H-, n-infix of the root *sey(H)- (“to put”).
From Latin situs (“position”), from a noun use of the perfect passive participle of sinō (“to put, lay”).
From Latin situs (“mold, filthiness”, literally “the state of having been left abandoned”), from a noun use of the perfect passive participle of sinō (“to put, lay”).

parole.significato: to situate, to place, to put, to locate, to set

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin situla (“vessel for water”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of secchia.
Learned borrowing from Latin sitientem, present active participle of sitiō (“to thirst”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sitiō (“to thirst”), from the words of Jesus on the cross (John 19:28).

parole.significato: to be restless, to be agitated, to be eager, to fidget

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin smaragdīnus. By surface analysis, smeraldo (“emerald”) + -ino (“-ine”, derivational suffix).
From Latin Smyrnaeus, Ancient Greek Σμυρναῖος (Smurnaîos).
Borrowed from Latin suāvitātem. By surface analysis, soave + -ità.
From Latin sōbrius (“sober”), from se- (“without”) + ēbrius (“intoxicated”).

Inherited from Latin societās via the nominative form. Doublet of società, a borrowing via the accusative societātem. The backwards shift in stress is slightly unusual; for the more normal result, cf. figliòlo < fīlìolus. Compare, for a similar output, Sicilian cìvita.
From Latin socius, from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare the doublet socio.
Learned borrowing from Latin soccus, from Ancient Greek σύκχος (súkkhos). Doublet of zocco.
From Latin sociālis (“of or pertaining to companionship; social”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, associate, companion”).

Borrowed from Latin societātem ("community, society", accusative form), from socius (“partner, ally”). By surface analysis, socio + -età. The senses of "association" and "company" were borrowed later. Doublet of soccida, which was inherited from the Latin nominative societās.
Borrowed from Latin sociābilis, remodeled based on -evole. By surface analysis, socio (“affiliate, fellow”) + -evole.

parole.significato: member, affiliate, partner, associate, fellow, mate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin socius (“partaking, associated; partner, associate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷyo- (“companion”), derived from the root *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare also the inherited soccio.
Borrowed from Latin sodālicium, from sodālicius (“pertaining to a fellowship”).

Inherited from Latin satisfacere. Once the first element satis (“enough”) had been lost as an independent word, the verb was remodelled according to the Italian prefixes so- and dis-, as if derived from a Latin *sub-dis-facere. Doublet of satisfare, a borrowing from Latin.
From earlier satisfatto, from Latin satisfactus, past participle form of satisfaciō (“reparation, amends”).
From Latin satisfactiōnem (“reparation, amends”). By surface analysis, soddisfa(re) (“to satisfy”) + -zione (“-tion”, noun-forming suffix).
Inherited with velar l-vocalization from Latin soldus, syncope of solidus (“solid”), from *solh₂- (“whole”). Doublet of solido and soldo.
Uncertain. Possibly from Latin supplicem, influenced by a Vulgar Latin *sufflectere, from Latin flectere.
Inherited from Latin suffulcīre (“to prop up”), with change of conjugation.
Borrowed from Latin sophus, from Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós, “wise”).
From Latin subiectīvus. Cognate with Piedmontese sogetiv.

parole.significato: to stand below, to be placed below

parole.testo: From Latin subiugātor. By surface analysis, soggiogare + -tore.
From Latin subiugātiō. By surface analysis, soggiogare + -zione.
From Latin solea. Compare French seuil.
From Latin solium (“seat, throne”), from Proto-Indo-European *sodyom, derived from *sed- (“to sit”).
From Latin somniāre (“to dream; to daydream”). By surface analysis, sogn(o) (“dream”) + -are (first conjugation verbal suffix).
From sognare + -tore, or from Latin somniātōrem.
From Latin somnium (“dream”), derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From the first syllable of Latin solve, from the medieval hymn Ut queant laxis, from which the names of the notes were derived.

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ostiolum. By surface analysis, uscio (“door”) + -olo (diminutive suffix).

Borrowed from Latin ūsus, perfect passive participle of ūtor (“to make use”).
Inherited from Latin ūsus (“use, employment”), from Proto-Italic *oissos.

parole.significato: to raptly look (typically at food) (typically of animals)
usucaption The acquisition of right or title to an object by means of the passage of time

parole.testo: From Latin ūsūra (“use; enjoyment”), derived from ūsus, perfect passive participle of ūtor (“to use; to enjoy”).

parole.significato: one who lends money at interest
parole.testo: From usura + -aio, corresponding to Latin ūsūrārius. Cf. also usurario.
Learned borrowing from Latin ūsūrārius. See also usuraio.
From Latin ūsūrpāre (“to use; to seize; to appropriate”).

Borrowed from Latin vaccīnus. Compare French vaccin. The meaning was based on that of New or Scientific Latin (variola) vaccīna.

parole.significato: to sway, to totter, to stagger along

Unadapted borrowing from Latin vāde mēcum (literally “Go with me!”).
Borrowed from Latin vadōsus (“full of shallows”).

parole.significato: to wander, to roam, to range
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vagārī (“to ramble, wander, stroll about”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna. Doublet of guaina.

parole.significato: to cry, to wail, to whimper (of a baby)

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin bāca (“berry, fruit”), with a change in gender.
Inherited from Latin varius. Doublet of vario, which was borrowed.
Borrowed from Latin valē (“be well, goodbye”).

parole.significato: to cross (a river, a border, a range of mountains, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vāricāre, from vāricus. Cf. also the doublet varcare.
Borrowed from Latin validitātem. By surface analysis, valido + -ità.

parole.significato: valid, effective, good, substantial, sound, strong

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vallāris, derived from vallum (“rampart, wall”).

parole.significato: to surround with a wall or rampart, to wall
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vallāre, derived from vallum (“rampart, wall”).
From Latin vallem, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Sicilian vaḍḍuni.

parole.significato: the wooden fence built at the top of a rampart

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vallus, diminutive of vannus (“winnowing basket”).
From Latin vapor (“steam; smoke”), influenced by lampo (“flash”).

From Latin vāricāre, from vāricus. Cf. also the doublet valicare.

parole.significato: to change, to vary, to diversify

parole.significato: vaso- (pertaining to blood vessels or the vascular system)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vassus, from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”).
From Latin vātēs (“prophet, poet”). Compare English vates.
From Latin vitulus (“bull calf”), probably through a Vulgar Latin form *vitlus, viclus.

parole.significato: vetch (many of the plants in the genus Vicia)

Inherited from Latin vidua, possibly through a Vulgar Latin *viduva.

From Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.

Inherited from Latin vindicta (“vengeance”), from vindico (“to claim, to vindicate”), from vindex (“defender”).

parole.significato: to avenge, to revenge, to take revenge for

Borrowed from Latin venerābilis, from venerārī.
Borrowed from Latin Venerālia, derived from Venus.
From Latin venerārī (“to worship, adore, revere, venerate”).
From Latin Veneris diēs, variant of diēs Veneris (“day of Venus”).
From Latin venereus, venerius (“of or relating to sexual love”), from Venus (“Roman goddess of love”) (from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”)) + -eus, -ius.

parole.significato: of Veneto (region of Italy); from Veneto

parole.testo: From vena + -oso, or from Latin vēnōsus. Cognate with Piedmontese venus.

parole.significato: wind (movement of air caused by differences in atmospheric pressure)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts, from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
From Latin ventōsus. By surface analysis, vento (“wind”) + -oso (“-y, -ous”). Cognate with Piedmontese ventus.

parole.significato: Ventôse (the sixth month of the French Republican Calendar)
parole.testo: Taken from Latin ventōsus (“windy”), as a calque of French ventôse.
Borrowed from Latin ventriculus. Doublet of ventriglio and ventricchio.
From Latin ventūra (“the things that will come”, i.e. “the future”), neuter plural form of ventūrus (“which will come”), future active participle of veniō (“to come, approach”).
From Latin ventūrus (“about to come”), future active participle of veniō (“to come, approach”).

parole.significato: beautiful in a specifically graceful way
beauty with a specific component of gracefulness, esp. said of feminine beauty
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin venustātem (“loveliness”, “beauty”), from Proto-Italic *wenostāts (“beauty”), from Proto-Indo-European *wénh₁osteh₂ts, ultimately from the root *wenh₁- (“to love”).
Borrowed from Latin verbēna. Compare the doublet vermena.
From Latin verbum (“word, verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from root *werh₁- (“to speak, to say”) + extension *-dʰ-.
From Latin verbōsus. Cognate with Piedmontese verbus.
Borrowed from Latin verecundia. Doublet of vergogna, which was inherited.
From Latin virga (“twig, stick”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *wisgeh₂ (“flexible rod or stick”).
Borrowed from Latin vergere (“to turn, incline”), from Proto-Italic *wergō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wérg-e-ti, derived from the root *h₂werg- (“to turn”).
Inherited from Latin virgula. Doublet of virgola, which was borrowed.

parole.significato: to verify, test, check, examine, inspect, survey

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vēritātem, in this form probably a semi-learned term which was altered based on the Latin etymology. The older, now obsolete forms vertà, vertade, and vertate were inherited.
From Latin verbēna. Compare also the doublet verbena.

parole.significato: to bring spring, to be vernal
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vernāre (“to be verdant; to be lively”).
Inherited from Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).
From Latin verres, with a change in declension.
From Latin versāre (“to turn, to twist”).
From Latin versārī (“to linger, to remain; to be engaged in”).
From Latin versātilis, from versāre (“to turn, to twist”).

parole.significato: having different, changing colors; versicoloured, varicoloured

parole.testo: From Latin versōria (“rope to adjust a sail”).
From Latin versus. Doublet of versus.
From Latin versus (past participle of vertere). Cognate to French vers (“towards”).
Borrowed from Latin versus. Doublet of verso, which is inherited.

parole.significato: to be about, turn on, concern

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vertīginōsus, derived from vertīgō.
From older vertude, from Latin virtūtem.
From Latin vērē ūnus (literally “truly only one”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vēsānia, derived from vēsānus (“mad, insane”).
From Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca.
Inherited from Latin episcopus, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos). Doublet of episcopo, a learned borrowing from the same source.
From Latin vesper. Doublet of ovest.

parole.significato: to vex, to oppress, to torment

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vexātōrem (“troubler, harasser”), derived from vexō.
From Latin vexātiōnem, derived from vexō.
Borrowed from Latin vēxillārius. By surface analysis, vessillo + -ario.
From Latin veterānus, probably a borrowing.

parole.significato: original or old-fashioned (used, especially, in a religious or political context)

parole.testo: From Latin vitrum, from Proto-Italic *wedrom, from Proto-Indo-European *wedro- (“water-like”), derived from the root *wed- (“water”). Cognate with French verre, Portuguese vidro, Spanish vidrio.

parole.significato: top, summit, crown (of a hill etc.)

parole.testo: From Latin vectōrem. Cognate with Piedmontese vetur.
Inherited from Latin vitium. Doublet of vizio, which was borrowed.
From vezzo + -oso or from Latin vitiōsus. Doublet of vizioso.
Borrowed from Latin viābilis. By surface analysis, via + -abile.

parole.significato: the communion administered as part of the last rites
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viāticum (“provision for a journey”), from the adjective viāticus (“pertaining to a journey”). Doublet of viaggio.

parole.significato: substitute, delegate, representative (someone who substitutes for or represents someone else of higher authority)
vicennial, occurring once every twenty years
parole.testo: From Latin vīcennālis, from vīcennium + -ālis, from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ium, from vīciēs (“twenty times”) + annus (“year”) + -is.

parole.significato: vicennalia (the festival and religious rituals celebrating a Roman emperor's 20th year of rule)
parole.testo: From Latin vīcennālia, neuter plural of vīcennālis.
From Latin vicennium (“20-year period”), from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ium, from vicies (“twenty each”) + annus (“year”) + -is. Cognate with Italian vicennale.

parole.significato: Vicentine (of, from or relating to Vicenza)
vice versa; the other way around; and back

parole.testo: From vicino + -ità or from Latin vīcīnitātem.
Inherited from Latin vīcus, from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“village, household”).

parole.significato: to forbid, to prohibit, to ban, to stop, to prevent

parole.testo: From Latin vetus (“old”), from Proto-Italic *wetos (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *wétos.

parole.significato: to be in force (of a law or regulation)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vigēre (“to be vigorous or thriving; thrive, flourish; to be in honor, esteem or repute; to prosper; to be alive, live”).
From Latin vīgēsimus, alternative form of vīcēsimus (“twentieth”) formed by analogy with vīgintī (“twenty”).

parole.significato: to supervise, to monitor, to guard, to keep an eye on
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vigilāre. Doublet of vegliare and vegghiare, which were borrowed from Occitan and inherited from Latin respectively.

parole.significato: residue obtained from the elimination of chaff from the beaten wheat
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vīlia, neuter plural of vīlis (“cheap”).
From Latin vīnētum, influenced by vigna.

parole.significato: to despise or scorn or vilipend
parole.testo: From Latin vilipendere, from vilis (“base, cheap”) and pendere (“to consider”).
From Latin vilipendium, from the verb vilipendo (whence also vilipendere).

parole.significato: pomace (pulp remaining from the process of winemaking)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vīnācea (“skin or husk of a grape”), noun use of the feminine form of vīnāceus (“of or pertaining to wine or a grape”, adjective).
From vino + -aio, or from Latin vīnārius.

From vincolo (“tie/bind”, noun) + -are, or borrowed from Latin vinculāre. Compare avvinghiare.
Borrowed from Latin vinculum (“bond, link”), from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -ulum. Compare the inherited doublet vinco.

parole.significato: wine (an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting grape juice, with an ABV ranging from 5.5–16%)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁nom, derived from *wéyh₁ō (“vine, wine”). Cognates include Albanian verë, Armenian գինի (gini) and Greek οίνος (oínos).

parole.significato: to break, violate, infringe, profane, run afoul of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin violāre (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”).
Borrowed from Latin violātiōnem (“injury, profanation”), from violō (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”).
Borrowed from Latin virgineus (whence also the form vergineo, which exhibits vowel dissimilation). By surface analysis, virgin- (“virgin”, fossilized stem for vergine) + -eo.
Borrowed from Latin virgula. Doublet of vergola, which was inherited.

parole.significato: viridarium, the garden of the patrician house
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viridārium. Doublet of verziere.
Learned borrowing from Latin virum (“man”), from Proto-Indo-European *wiHrós.
From Latin viriola (“little bracelet”), diminutive of viria (“bracelet”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *weiros (“crooked”).

From Latin vīsitāre (“to see, to visit”), frequentative of visō.
From Latin vīsitātiōnem. By surface analysis, visitare + -zione.
Inherited from Latin vīsum. Compare the doublet avviso.

parole.significato: viewer; apparatus for viewing (slides, microfilm, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin vīsōrem (“viewer, watcher”) from videō (“to view, watch”), from Proto-Italic *widēō (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”).
From Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā, possibly a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂, from the root *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”).

parole.significato: old man's beard, traveller's joy/traveler's joy (Clematis vitalba)
parole.testo: From vite alba or Latin vītis alba (“white vine”).
From vita + -ale, or from Latin vītālis.
Borrowed from Latin vītandus, gerundive of vītō (“to avoid”).
From Latin vitellus. Compare Romanian vițel, French veau, Catalan vedella .
From Latin vitilīgō (“cutaneous eruption, tetter”), from vitium (“defect, blemish”).
Borrowed from Latin victōria, from vincere.
Borrowed from Latin victōriōsus. By surface analysis, vittoria (“victory”) + -oso.
From Latin vĭtŭpĕrābĭlis. By surface analysis, vituperare + -abile.
From Latin vīvācitātem, probably a borrowing. By surface analysis, vivace + -ità.
From Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).
From Latin vīvidus (“alive; lively”), derived from the verb vīvō (“to am alive, live”).
From Latin vīvus (“alive”, “living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
Borrowed from Latin vitiāre. Cognate with Piedmontese vissié, Spanish / Portuguese viciar, French vicier. Compare English vitiate.

Inherited from Latin volāre, from Proto-Italic *gʷelāō.

parole.significato: to be affectionate (to), to feel affection or love (for); to care (for/about); to be fond (of)
parole.testo: From Latin benē volō. Literally, “to wish well”.

parole.significato: to turn, to direct (something (towards a specific object or goal))

From Latin vultus (“expression, face”). Compare Portuguese vulto (“aspect”).
Borrowed from Latin volūta, from the feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō.

parole.significato: volva (cup-shaped mass at the base of various fungi)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin volva, alternative form of vulva.

parole.significato: a sinkhole formed by the erosion of water or by the collapse of a cave's vault
parole.testo: Derived from Latin vorō (“to devour, swallow up”).

Inherited from Latin vostrum, which is the accusative of voster, which derives from the older form vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.

parole.significato: to vote [with per ‘for’; or with a favore di ‘in favor of’; or with contro ‘against’]
parole.testo: Derived from Latin vōtum, from voveō. Compare Spanish and Portuguese votar, French vouer.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter V/v.; vee
parole.testo: From Latin ū (the name of the letter V).
From Vulcano (“Vulcano, a complex stratovolcano in the Mediterranean”), from Latin Vulcānus (“Vulcan”).

Borrowed from Latin vulnerāre (“to wound, injure”), derived from vulnus (“wound”).
Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, from earlier volva, from the Proto-Indo-European root *welH- (“to turn, wind”).
From Latin Zacynthius, from Ancient Greek Ζακύνθιος (Zakúnthios), from Ζάκυνθος (Zákunthos, “Zakynthos”). By surface analysis, Zacinto + -io.

From Latin symphōnia (possibly influenced, through folk etymology, by zampa (“paw, leg of an animal”) in Italian, as bagpipes are traditionally made of leather with the hair still on), from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). From Latin zancha (a kind of shoe), from Parthian.

parole.significato: an agricultural implement, such as a hoe

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter Z/z.; zed, zee
parole.testo: From the Latin zēta, from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta), from Hebrew זין (zayin).

From a- + sottile (“thin”) + -are, or from a- + sottigliare (now obsolete), from Late Latin subtiliāre, from Latin subtīlis.

parole.significato: to equip, to fit out, to tool up
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from attrezzo, itself possibly from French attraits. Alternatively from Vulgar Latin *attrectiāre, from Latin attrectāre.
From Latin vīvācius, comparative form of vīvāciter (“vigorously”), from vīvāx (“vigorous, lively”). Compare Catalan aviat. Alternatively from Latin vīvāciter.
From balza or possibly a Vulgar Latin root *balteanus, from Latin balteus. Compare also Old French bauçant.

Less likely from Provençal brau (“show-off”), from Gaulish *bragos (compare Middle Irish breagha (modern breá) 'fine', Breton braga 'to strut'). Or perhaps borrowed from a descendant of Proto-Germanic *hrawaz

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burius (“red, dark”), either from Latin burrus (“reddish-brown”) or, less likely, from Latin furvus (“dark, dusky”).

Traditionally believed to derive from Latin būris (“beam of the plow”), used by farmers and thus associated with countryside people; alternatively, perhaps, from Lombardic būr (“peasant”). Either way suffixed with -ino.

Perhaps from Ancient Greek βοτήρ (botḗr, “herdsman”), akin to βόσκω (bóskō, “to graze”). Alternatively from Ancient Greek βούτης (boútēs, “yokel”), from βοῦς (boûs, “cattle”). Caix derives it from Vulgar Latin puttulus, diminutive of puttus, from Latin putus (“boy”), since the meaning is still prese
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek καλαϕατέω (kalaphatéō) or from Arabic قَلْفَطَ (qalfaṭa, “to caulk (a ship)”), both from Latin calefaciō (“to heat”).
From caldara (cf. caldaia), with the suffix -one, or from a derivative of Latin caldarium, Late Latin caldaria. Compare French chaudron, Portuguese caldeirão, Spanish calderón.
From caldo or from a Vulgar Latin root *caldūra, from Latin caldus, calidus. Compare Romanian căldură.

Deverbal from cambiare + -o. From verb cambiare inherited from Vulgar Latin cambiāre (“to change, exchange”) from Late Latin cambiō, or from corresponding noun Latin cambium (“change”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”). Compare Spanish cambio and Portuguese câmbio.
From cancello + -iere, or from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancellus. Cognate with Sicilian canciḍḍeri.

parole.significato: complexion (appearance of the skin on the face)
parole.testo: From carne or from a Late Latin carnātiōnem, from Latin carō.
From catena (“chain, bond”) + -accio, or from Late Latin catēnāceum, from Latin catēna.
Probably borrowed from Portuguese cabo or from Genoese, ultimately from Latin capulum.

parole.significato: to hoop (put hoops around a barrel, etc.)
parole.testo: From cerchio + -are, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *circlāre < Late Latin circulāre, from Latin circulārī, and therefore doublet of the borrowing circolare. Compare French cercler.
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin īsicia, plural of īsicium (“minced meat”), from īnsicium < Latin īnsecō (“cut up”). Compare Spanish chicha. Alternatively, from a syncope of carniccia.

From the variant ciriegia, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin. parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; alternatively; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps of Germanic origin; cf. German Schutt (“rubble”). Alternatively from Latin cautēs (“rough pointed rock”), via a Gallo-Italic language (hence the palatalization of /ka-/) with a change in gender and notable reduction in size. Either way, cognate with Romagnol ẓòt.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Several theories exist. Possibly from a central-northern Italian word (cf. cocón) ultimately derived from Latin calcāre (“to press”), or from a derivative of Latin caucus, from Ancient Greek káukē. Alternatively, from a corchiume, related to Spanish corcho (cf. English cork), from Latin c
From comprare + -tore, or from Late Latin comparātōrem, from Latin comparō.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, itself either from Latin datum (“thrown, given”), or from Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese dado, Catalan dau, French dé (whence English die).
From Latin diatonicus or from French diatonique.

From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin ieiūnium. The initial Latin ie- or je- may have changed to de- over time, leading to di- in Italian. Compare the similar Catalan dejuni. Alternatively digiuno may have been regressively derived from the verb digiunare, and was independent of this Latin word.

parole.significato: to issue, to put out, to release, to disseminate (an invitation, press release, etc.)
parole.testo: From di- + ramo, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Romanian dărâma, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.

Probably a back-formation of doccione (“conduit, spout”), from Latin ductiōnem, from ducere, infinitive of dūcō (“lead, guide; draw, pull”), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *ducea, ultimately from the same root. Compare Dozza, a borrowing from Emilian Dòza.
From doglia + -oso or from a Vulgar Latin root *doliōsus, from Latin dolor. Compare Romanian duios, Friulian duliôs.

Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.
From Latin phaseolus, probably from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos) or from Ancient Greek φασούλια (phasoúlia). Unrelated to fava.

parole.significato: to fail to germinate (of a seed)
parole.testo: From fallo + -are or falla + -are, from Vulgar Latin *falla, or from Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.

Perhaps from Old Italian parpaglione, from Latin papiliō (“butterfly”). Compare Old French paveillon, Catalan papalló, Provençal parpalhos, Lombard parpaja. The f is difficult to account for, though it might be due to the Tuscan gorgia. Alternatively, from the dialectal Arabic word in Maltese farfet

Inherited from Latin forficula (“small scissors”), from forfic- (“scissors”) + -ula, with an unexpected shift of the first vowel. Compare borrowed doublet forficula and seemingly inherited doublet forfecchia (“earwig”). Alternatively, possibly from the Osco-Umbrian substrate, from Proto-Italic *farð
Either borrowed from Latin pharmacum, or from its source, Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon).
Borrowed from Occitan fermalh or from French fermail, in either case from Vulgar Latin *firmāc(u)lum, derived from Latin firmāre (“make fast”).
From ferro (“iron”) + -are, or from a Late Latin ferrāre (cf. Classical Latin ferrātus), from Latin ferrum. Compare French ferrer, Catalan and Portuguese ferrar, Spanish herrar.
Inherited from Latin fābula (> ˈfabla > 'fabbja > ˈfjabᵇa), or alternatively through a Vulgar Latin form *flaba from metathesis of *fabla. Doublet of favola and fola.
Uncertain, either derived from filo or, perhaps, from an unattested earlier *filzella, from Vulgar Latin *filicella, from Latin fīlum

From forno + -ello (“diminutive suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Sicilian furneddu, Catalan fornell, Romansh furnel, Sardinian furredhu, Occitan fornèl, Portuguese fornilho, Spanish hornillo.
From fritto + -ura, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīctus. Compare French friture, Romanian friptură, Spanish and Portuguese fritura, Sicilian frittura.
From fumo + -aiolo, or from Late Latin fūmāriolum, from Latin fūmārium, from fūmus.

Possibly of Germanic origin, or from Latin vagus (“wandering, flighty, giddy”); likely of the same genesis as Old Occitan gai, whence cognate to French gai, Portuguese gaio and English gay. Cognate with Sicilian javiu.

parole.significato: cuckoopint, arum (Arum genus and species, especially Arum maculatum)
parole.testo: Unknown. The only attestation in Latin presents it as Gaulish: c. 400, Marcellus Empiricus, De medicamentis, 10:58: Polypum emendat herba proserpinalis, quae Graece draconteum, Gallice gigarus appellatur, vel sucus eius naribus infundatur vel si papyrus inde infecta et spicillo involuta naribus inse
From giudicare (“to judge”) + -mento (“-ment”), or possibly from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Compare Spanish juzgamiento, Portuguese julgamento, Catalan jutjament, French jugement.
From gocciare or from a Vulgar Latin *guttia or *guttea; ultimately from Latin gutta.

From gargozza, or gargozzo, itself from an onomatopoeic root garg- or from Vulgar Latin *gurgutia or *gargutium. Another etymology proposed is *guttium, variant of Latin guttur (“throat”), confused with guttus (“jug”). Alternatively, possibly from a derivative Vulgar Latin *gusia (compare French gos
Probably from grovigliolo, from an alteration of rubiglio. Or possibly connected with Latin globus via a Vulgar Latin *globilia.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin gruma, from Latin grumus, or alternatively of Germanic origin.
From im (“in”) + bocca (“mouth”) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca. Compare Spanish and Catalan embocar, French emboucher, Romanian îmbuca.

Deverbal from ingombrare + -o. parole.significato: to turn green, to green, to make green
parole.testo: Either from in- + verde + -ire, or from a Vulgar Latin *invir(i)dire, from *invir(i)descere, from Latin viridēscere. Compare Romanian înverzi, Catalan enverdir, Spanish enverdir, enverdecer, Portuguese enverdecer, French verdir.
From lavare + -tura, or from a Vulgar Latin *lavatūra, from Latin lavō. Compare French lavure, Sicilian lavatura, Spanish lavadura, Romanian lături.

From Latin iūlius, through a process of dissimilation; compare also the obsolete regional variant form giuglio. Alternatively, derived from a Vulgar Latin root *lūlius, along with other Italo-Romance and Rhaeto-Romance cognates; compare Corsican lugliu, Neapolitan lùglio, Sicilian lugghiu, Venetan l

parole.significato: a charge consisting of four crescents arrranged in a ring
parole.testo: Borrowed either from Spanish lunel or directly from French lunel, ultimately based on Latin lūna (“moon”).
Borrowed from Old French madrier or from Old Occitan madier, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *māterium, from Latin māteria (“matter; timber”).
From Latin mānsiōnem, either inherited or borrowed from Old French maison.

parole.significato: to be lacking, to be missing (of objects)
parole.testo: From manco (adjective) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus.
From Late Latin martellus, diminutive of martulus, variant of Latin marculus, diminutive of marcus, or from malleus (“hammer”). Compare Portguese martelo and Catalan martell.
Inherited from Late Latin mascara, *mascra, masca. Doublet of mascara.

From Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), itself either from a contraction of a form *madĭtus (as a past participle of Latin madeō), or madidus (“drunk, tipsy”). Cognate to French mat (“matte, pale”).
From minuzzare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiālia, from Latin minūtia. Compare Friulian minuçae, Old French menuisaille, Portuguese miuçalha, Aromanian minutsalji.
From minuzza /minuzzare + -ame or from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiamen, from Latin minūtia.

parole.testo: Etymology uncertain, possibly either: * from mozzo (“cut off; shortened”, adjective) (from Vulgar Latin *mutius, from Latin mutilus (“mutilated”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mewt- (“cut short”)); or * from Late Latin almucia (“hood or cape with a hood worn by cle

From Latin mūtulus, syncopated to *mutlus, or from cumulus, transposed to a Vulgar Latin form *muculus > *muclus. Based on the first etymology, mutulo is a doublet, and based on the second, cumulo and cumolo are.

Uncertain; either from Vulgar Latin *nīdiculāre (“to stay in one's nest”), from Latin nīdus (“nest”), or from Vulgar Latin *hinnitulāre, from Latin hinniō (“to neigh, whinny”), possibly even from a merger of the two.

From the feminine of the past participle of offrire, or from Medieval Latin or Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Sardinian oferta; Friulian ufierte; Romansh offerta; Sicilian ufferta.
From Latin olīva, from Etruscan 𐌄𐌋𐌄𐌉𐌅𐌀 (eleiva) or from Proto-Hellenic *elaíwā (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀨𐀷 (e-ra-wa), Ancient Greek ἐλαίᾱ (elaíā)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁loywom.
From oliva or from Vulgar Latin olīvus, from Latin olīva, olīvum.

Feminine of palombo or from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain, but probably from the older variant palanco or from palanca, from Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin paranchus, palanchus. Cognate with Sicilian parànculu.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *pedinus, a derivative of Latin pedem (“foot”). Compare Sicilian pèdinu, Romanian piedin, Albanian pedim. Alternatively from Latin pendulus. Less likely linked to penna / pinna (“feather”).
From penzolo + -are or from Vulgar Latin *pendiolāre, from *pendiolus, from Latin pendulus, from pendō.
Borrowed from Occitan perilh or French péril, in either case from Latin perīculum, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to go forth, forwards”). Doublet of pericolo.

Probably from Latin petīgō ("scab, eruption"), a popular form of impetīgo (perhaps through a Vulgar Latin root *peticla < *(im)peticula, or alternatively, from a Vulgar Latin *pestic(u)la, from pestis. Less likely from Ancient Greek πιττάκια (pittákia), plural of πιττάκιον (pittákion).

parole.significato: henhouse, chicken coop, chicken run, roost
parole.testo: From pollo + -aio, or from Late Latin pullārium, from Latin pullārius (“pertaining to young animals or chicks”), from pullus (“young animal, chick”). Compare also pollario.

parole.significato: In the Roman Empire, the tract of land denoting the formal, sacral ambit of a Roman city
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pōmoerium, pōmērium (“the religious boundary of a city”), which word being either formed as post (“behind”) + moerus, mūrus (“wall”) + -ium (neuter form of -ius, adjectival suffix) or derived from Etruscan [Term?].
From pomo + -eto or from Late Latin pomētum, from Latin pomus. Compare Romanian pomet.
Either deverbal from provare (“to try; to test; to prove; to feel”) + -a, or from Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.
From pugno, or from a Vulgar Latin *pūgnālis, from Latin pugnus. Compare Spanish puñal, Portuguese punhal, Catalan punyal, French poignard (Old French poignal).

parole.significato: flagship of a fleet personally commanded by a king or viceroy (pre-18th c.)
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Old French reial, from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”), or inherited from Latin rēgālis with possible influence from French. Doublet of regale.
From Old French rihote, perhaps related to riboter or from Latin rugiō (“to roar”).

parole.significato: to restore, to turn around, to balance, to reorganize
parole.testo: From ri- + sanare, or from Late Latin resānāre, from Latin sānāre. Compare Spanish resanar.

parole.significato: to twist again, to retwist (wire, etc.)
parole.testo: From ri- + torcere (“to twist”), or from Vulgar Latin *retorcere, from Latin retorquēre.

Perhaps from Latin aerūginem (“rust”), from aes, aeris (“bronze”) + -ūgō (forms nouns denoting superficial coatings). Or possibly from Late Latin arānea (originally spider's web, later coming to refer to skin diseases such as herpes, scabies, impetigo, etc.) crossed with rodere (“to gnaw”) into a Vu
Uncertain, probably from a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin roncus or ronchus, of Ancient Greek origin, or alternatively a root *runcus, from Latin runcō.
Probably from a derivative of Latin rebellāre or from arrovellare. Another possibility is Latin rubellus, diminutive of ruber.
From sabbia + -one or from Late Latin sablōnem, from Latin sabulōnem. Compare archaic French sablon.
From sale (“salt”) + -are (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix), or from a Vulgar Latin *salāre, changed in conjugation from Latin salīre.
Borrowed from Latin sarcoma, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + -ωμα (-ōma, “process”) or from Ancient Greek σαρκόω (sarkóō), itself from σάρξ (sárx).
From s- + battere, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *exbattere, from Latin battuere.

Derived regressively from the verb scalzare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *excalceus, itself either from a shortening of Latin excalceatus, or from ex- + calceus. parole.significato: to lose, to suffer a loss [with di] (economically, morally, etc.)
parole.testo: Possibly from a Late Latin excapitāre (which meant "decapitate" in its attested form, but the Romance descendants may derive from an unattested sense of "to conclude, finish, reach the end of" which developed later, or possibly "to decrease, diminish"), a derivation of Latin caput, or from capitare,
Borrowed from French écharpe, from Old French escharpe, from Frankish *skirpa (“bandoleer”), of either Germanic or Latin origin.
Formed from Latin secundus, or from Latin secundāre.
From Turkish saray or from Vulgar Latin serrāculum, from a late form of Latin serāre (“lock up, close”), from sera (“lock, bolt”).
From sotterra + -are, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *subterrāre, from Latin sub- + terra.

From s- + penzolo or penzolare. Alternatively possibly from s- (< Latin ex) + a Vulgar Latin root *pendiolāre, from *pendiolus, from pendulus, from Latin pendō, or *expendiolāre. Compare Romanian spânzura.
From sperare + -anza, or from Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare French espérance, Spanish esperanza, Portuguese esperança

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *disperdicāre, from Latin disperdere, or from Vulgar Latin *dispergicāre, iterative of Latin dispergere, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *exprecāre ("drive into ruin"), from Latin ex- + precāri.

Either from Vulgar Latin *extentāre, from Latin tentāre, or from s- (from Latin Latin ex-) + tentare (from Latin temptāre), or from Vulgar Latin *abstentāre, from Latin abstentum, from abstineō. Cognate with Friulian stentâ, Lombard stentà, Piedmontese stenté.
From stoppa + -are or from Vulgar Latin *stuppāre, from Latin stuppa. Compare Venetan stupar, Sicilian stuppari, Romansh stuppar, French étouper, Old Spanish estopar, Romanian astupa.
Borrowed from Japanese 天麩羅 (てんぷら, tenpura), from Portuguese, ultimately from Latin, cognate with either temperare or tempo, tempora. See above for more.
From terra, or from Vulgar Latin *terraceus, from Latin terra. Related to terrazza. Cf. also terraccio, terracia. Compare Spanish terrazo.
From Latin texere, from Proto-Italic *teksō, either from Proto-Indo-European *tḗtḱ-ti or from *teḱ-se-ti, both from *teḱ- (“to beget, produce”).

parole.significato: to blank, shear, or trench (sheet metal)
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *trīnicāre, from trīnī + root of duplicō, or from an alternation of Latin truncāre.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; alternatively; or possibly
parole.testo: From Late Latin troia, troja, of uncertain origin, but possibly: * from Latin (porcum de) Troia (“(hog of) Troy”), after the Trojan horse, * or alternatively of Celtic origin, from a Gaulish root *trogja, from a root meaning “to pull” and thence also “fertile," Proto-Celtic *trāglo-, for which see L
From unghia (“nail, claw”) + -ato, or from Late Latin ungulātus, from Latin ungula.
From vedova, vedovo + -are, or from Late Latin viduāre, from Latin viduus.
Borrowed from Occitan ventrelh, or from Old French ventreil, in either case from Latin ventriculus (“belly”). Compare the doublets ventricolo and ventricchio.

Uncertain. Most sources originate it from Late Latin faluppa (“chaff, waste”) (from which also the doublet faloppa), influenced from/crossed with a derivate of Latin volvere. Other sources theorizes a sole derivation from volvere. Lastly, it may be related to/based on Old French (en)velopper, which
Uncertain, but possibly from Vulgar Latin *vincidus, itself likely derived from Latin vinciō (“tie, restrain”), or alternatively an alteration of viscido.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīsitus, from Latin vīsus, or from a form *vīditus.
From Latin volō through a Vulgar Latin root *volia, or from voglio. Cf. also Romanian voie from root *volia

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volta, from *volŭta (perhaps via *volvita (“a turn”)), from Latin volūta, feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Also possibly from the past participle of volgere (volto), or from the verb voltare. Compare Spanish vuelta; cf. also Spanish bóveda, Frenc
